subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.

speechtext: Right Hon.Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime * Minister): I deem it my duty to make a statement to the House with-respect to an item which has appeared in the press of the country touching a despatch received from the Secretary of State for the Colonies at the end of last week, which was given out to the press in the ordinary course.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: Received from and by whom?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext:
Received from the Secretary of State for_ the Colonies. About the middle of January last I suggested to the British Government, through the Secretary of State for the Colonies, that

it would be desirable to have a weekly resume, Or summary, of the war situation, which should be issued under the authority of the War Cabinet, and which might be published. We had been receiving for some time secret reports, which, of course, could not be made public, and the information set forth in those_ weekly reports was communicated only to members of the Administration, and in some cases to the Prime Minister alone.
We received a reply intimating that the matter would be taken into consideration, and about the end of March we were informed that such a despatch for publication would be sent to us weekly in the early future. These despatches began t-o come in about the end of March, or a little after, and when received they were published as was intended. They were not sent in code, and they were marked as official news for publication. It is understood that one of the Dominions of the Empire made a suggestion about two or three weeks ago that these news summaries were not as valuable as they might be for the reason that they set forth for the most part matters that had already been published in the press of the country. On Saturday last, one of those official news despatches was received in the ordinary course through His Excellency the Governor General, signed, as all these despatches are signed, by the Secretary of State for the Colonies, the Eight Hon. Walter Long. It was handed out to the press and published in the usual w>ay. Yesterday a further despatch correcting it in one respect was received in the same manner from the same source, and signed in the same way. That also has been given to the press. In communicating to the British Government in January last, we asked that these despatches might be sent to us under the authority of the War Cabinet. 1 do not know, of course, whether or not this particular despatch was sent out under the authority of the War Cabinet. I am content to accept the statement of Lord Beading in that behalf; he doubtless has more information on the subject than I have. What I desire to .make clear to the House and to the country is that the despatch in question was received in the ordinary course under the arrangement alluded to, and purported to be signed by the Secretary of State for the Colonies'. It was received through His Excellency the Governor 'General, and the despatch which corrected it was received in the same man-125
ner through the same source and signed in the same way. My purpose in making this statement is to assure Parliament and this country that if there has been any mistake or misapprehension with regard to this official news despatch it has not occurred here at Ottawa; it has occurred somewhere else.

On the Orders of the Day:

I
desire to rise to a question of privilege. Yesterday's Ottawa Citizen contains the following article, headed "Absolutely Untrue; Chief Justice on Dr. Edwards' Charges in the Commons":
"I do not know that I have very much to say about the charge of Dr. Edwards, except that it is absolutely untrue," stated Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, chief justice of Canada yesterday.
"I do not receive any such salary," stated Sir Charles. "The amount voted by parliament now is for travelling expenses when I go to Bondon as a member of the Judicial Committee. When I don't go I do not draw the allowance. There was one year when I drew it. At that time the amount was voted expressly without reference to expenses. It was a statutory allowance in connection with the position, the same as the amount allowed in my capacity as deputy of the Governor General. Afterwards the statute was changed to make the vote cover travelling expenses. When I don't go to Bondon why, of course, I do not receive the money."
My statement, to which exception was taken, may be found in Hansard of May 13, andi is as follows:

$2,500 a year was voted to a certain gentleman, whom I am not permitted to mention, for a specific purpose, which that gentleman did not carry out. The money was voted and taken. The next year the money was again voted and taken for that specific purpose, although that specific purpose was not carried out. The third year the money was voted for the same specific purpose, which purpose again was not carried out, but the money was taken.
. That is the statement which the gentleman in question says is absolutely untrue. The Appropriation Act and the Auditor General's Report show that for the year 1915-16 a vote of $2,500 was put through in these words :
Travelling expenses of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
The Auditor General's Report, page U3, shows that that amount was drawn. The next year the vote was similarly worded, and the Auditor General's Report, page U3, shows that the amount was taken. The next year, 1917-18, the wording was slightly changed to read:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
That amount was not drawn. According to the Appropriation Acts and the Auditor General's Report, the amount was drawn in two of the three years. My statement cannot be characterized as absolutely untrue; at least it is two-thirds true, while the assertion	in the press of the
gentleman in question can only be taken as fifty per cent true. I am willing to place my veracity on that basis against that of the Chief Justice of Canada, at all events, so far as principle is concerned -and that is the point wherein my veracity is called to question. The amount was taken for services which were not performed, and that is what I stated in the House. That was the principle involved, and admission has been made to that effect. As a matter of principle, it does not matter whether the amount wrongfully taken was $5,000 or $7,500. It has been admitted that $5,000 has been taken for which-

On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Finance), Bill No. 82, to amend the Inland Revenue Act was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-duties of excise on manufactured tobacco:

Does this include the
whole section?
Yes.

Will the minister give an explanation of the difference between clauses (a) and (b)? Clause (a) enumerates a number of tobaccos such as fine-cut, cavendish, plug or twist. Clause (b) says:
(b) On common Canada twist, when made solely from tobacco grown in Canada, and on the farm or premises where grown, by the cultivator duly licensed therefor, or in a licensed tobacco manufactory, twenty cents per pound, attua! weight.
If it is manufactured into chewing tobacco or otherwise the duty is 20 cents per

pound. I do not -quite understand the distinction that is drawn here.
This is tobacco twist made from the.'Canadian grown leal. The duty has been raised from ten to twenty *cents.
What is meant by the words " on common Canada twist when made solely from tobacco grown in Canada?"
That is a Canadian tobacco.
It -goes on to say " when made on the farm or premises where grown." Surely, it would not be grown in ,a factory.

The twist may (be made in a factory. It is also frequently made on the farm.
. iMr. McOOIiG: Is there any provision covering the point I raised the other day as to the duty being remitted on tobacco damaged by frost or otherwise?
There is nothing in the Bill which specifically covers that point, but there is a regulation now in force which provides that the duty shall not be exacted where the leaf has been destroyed.
Does this section mean that a farmer who grows tobacco and makes it into twist for himself and his family is exempt from paying the duty?
Thirty pounds are allowed to the grower for every male adult of his family.

Does the minister think it is fair to charge a duty of six dollars a thousand on cigars regardless of quality? That duty would be all- right on cigars costing seventy-five or a hundred dollars a thousand, but on the cheaper cigars costing from eighteen to forty dollars a thousand, does the minister not think the duty is too high?

The increased
duty upon cigars amounts to two-thirds or a cent per cigar. In the case of the five cent cigar the profit of the rfrtailer now is forty per cent. With the increased duty it will (be twenty per cent,, or a little over. There is some objection, possibly fair, from the trade in respect to the duty on the cheaper cigar. In the United States the duty is based on the" selling price, but that has not been the practice in Canada; we
have always charged on the quantity. If the tax is too onerous in the case of the cheaper cigar, we will reconsider the matter before the next session of Parliament.

I think the minister should increase the duty on the more expensive cigars selling at $150 per thousand', we will say. The margin between the wholesale and retail price on the five-cent cigar is so small that with the duty it will have to sell at six or seven cents; that is the cigar the workingman and the farmer smokes.
I think the minister would get more duty if he increased the tax to ten dollars per thousand on the higher-pricedi cigar and decreased it to two or three dollars per thousand in the case of the cheaper cigar.
The purpose of the tax is to raise revenue, and if we impose too high a tax, consumption will cease and there will be no revenue.

I do not admit that. I am sure the minister when he goes into a store does not buy the five-cent cigar of the workingman, selling at six for .a quarter, but a brand selling at three for fifty. If he chooses to smoke that quality of cigar, let him pay for the luxury. He is better able . to pay the duty than the workingman. I again repeat, the minister should increase the duty on the higher-priced cigar, and reduce it on the lower-priced, cigar.
I can promise my hon. friend that before the next session of Parliament we will reconsider the duty on the five-cent cigar.

The minister admits I have good grounds for my appeal to him. Why not reconsider the duty now? This is the proper time when we are passing the Bill. If the minister will not meet the farmers in the House, at least he should allow them to get .a cigar at a reasonable price.

Would it not be well for the Acting Minister of Finance to consider the advisability of putting excise duties on an ad( valorem instead of on a specific basis? I believe we are going to have very high taxation in this country in the future. In the past the excise and other duties have all been of .a more or less trifling character, except the tax on liquors, but now we have to face the practical inevitability of heavy taxation all along the line. Reasoning by analogy, a duty of ten cents per pound on tea is equivalent to a duty of twenty-five per cent on the tea used by working people, selling at around thirty cents a pound, hut it only works out

to about twenty per cent, in ,the case of the higher-priced1 tea. I am merely arguing by analogy, but it seems to me the principle ;s a correct one, and I would join with my hon. friend from Richmond and Wolfe in urging on the Acting Minister of Finance the advisability of starting out right in regard to these taxes, because, after all, it is new conditions we are called upon to meet. I think it was the Acting Minister of Finance himself who said the other day that it was a condition and not a theory that confronted us. Being confronted with new conditions, I would urge on the Government the advisability of meeting those conditions by starting the new regime of taxation on a just and reasonable basis. I believe the House is with me entirely when 1 say that the principle and1 the practice of ad valorem duties is more reasonable than specific duties. Specific duties usually work out so as to place the heavier burden on the poorer people of the country.
Does my hon. friend advocate an ad valorem duty on tea?

I am not advocating any certain ad valorem duty. I am not attempting to advise the Acting Minister of Finance as to the amount of any duty that he should place upon any article. I am -laying down a principle and it is a just and right one. That principle is that we should have our duties apportioned on an ad valorem basis and not on a specific basis.	[DOT]

Possibly the acting minister did not understand my point in reference to a damaged crop. A damaged crop very frequently sells for about one-quarter of what the crop would have sold for had it not been damaged. The argument of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) would apply to a very large extent to the point I was trying to make. If the producer had to depend upon selling his tobacco, a duty of five cents a pound would have a discouraging effect on the industry.

Under subsection 6 of section 2 of the Bill we are taking power to make regulations which will cover the point my hon. friend has mentioned, as well as other possible conditions which may arise to reduce the value of the home grown tobacco below the market price. We will keep this point in mind when the regulations are being framed.

If the minister assures the producers of tobacco that there will be regulations governing those cases, it will

largely assist in increasing the acreage which may be put under tobacco in Ontario this year.

I can assure my hon. friend that due provision will be made to cover the case he points out, and I would
be obliged if he would write a letter covering the point fully, to the Minister of Excise and .Customs.
On section 2-license to grow tobacco; fee; excise duty; exemption if tobacco grown for personal or family use; limited quantity free of duty; regulations; penalty:

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to subsection 6. He stated that regulations would be made in regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig). I doubt if he has power under that subsection to make those regulations. The subsection says:
The Minister charged with the collection of the tax imposed under this section shall have power to make such regulations as he deems necessary or advisable for carrying out the provisions of this section.
I do not think he has any general power to make regulations.

It says:
The Minister charged with the collection of the tax imposed under this section shall have power to make such regulations as he deems necessary or advisable for carrying out the provisions of this section.
I do not think that is definite enough to give the minister power.
The point is that the tax of 20 cents a pound is imposed under section 279 of the Inland Revenue Act.
The tax of five cents per pound is under subsection 3, of section 2, of the Bill. I think it is clear enough.

Under section 279 of the Act, subsection lb, on common twist tobacco, Canadian grown, there is an excise duty, or tax, of 20 cents a pound actual weight. The hon. member for Kent has drawn the attention of the Committee to the fact that often the tobacco which is grown is so much damaged that the crop will only realize five or ten cents a pound, which would be half the amount of the tax. The minister says that he can obviate that injustice by availing himself of the power under subsection 6 of section 328a; but subsection 6 of 328a only allows him, according to my reading of the provision, to make regulations regarding the collection

of. the taxes imposed under this section, 328a, while the tax of 20 -cents a pound on common Canada twist is imposed under section 279.

Yes, but that is manufactured tobacco, and that could not relate to tobacco that had been damaged. One refers to the tobacco leaf and the other to common twist tobacco that is manufactured. I read it so; I do not think there would toe any damaged Canadian leaf in it.

I do not think there should be any doubt about this. It seems to me that the tax which is referred to in subsection 6 of -section 328a is the tax imposed by subsection 3:
There shall be levied, collected and paid an excise duty on all tobacco grown in Canada for consumption therein of -five cents per pound, computed according to the standard of leaf tobacco as hereinbefore established.
That appears to be the tax that is referred -to in subsection 6 of -the same section, and not the tax that is referred to in subsection b of section 279.

That is quite correct, but -the hon. member for Kent was referring to Canadian leaf tobacco under subsection b of section 279.
Mr. McMASyEK: I do not think he was.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. M-oCoig) referred to the Canadian grown leaf, which is subject to the excise tax of five cents a pound, and he inquired if, when the leaf was damaged or destroyed, there might be a remission or rebate of duty, ail-d I answered him that the regulations would contain such power. The Inland Revenue Act, which, however, I have not before me, contains a stronger provision even than this, also enabling the department to make regulations which would cover the point.
(Mr. DEMERS: Does subsection 6 of section 328A apply to section 279?
*Mr'. A. K. MACLEAN: No.
So, th-ere is no answer to the question asked by the member for Kent?

The tobacco to which the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) referred had reference to Canadian tobacco leaf, on which there is imposed a tax of five cents a pound. That is what is referred -to in -section 328A.

The point I wish to make is this: Paragraph 3 of section 328A provides:
There shall be levied, collected and paid, an excise duty on all tobacco grown in Canada for consumption therein of five cents per pound, computed according to the standard .of leaf* tobacco as hereinbefore established.
Subsection 6 provides:
The Minister charged with the collection of the tax imposed under this section shall have power to make such regulations as he deems necessary or advisable for carrying out the provisions of this section.
Now the section which I have quoted provides that five cents a pound must be collected on leaf -tobacco, -and the power given under subsection 6 to make regulations has to do with the collection of that tax. The minister has no power to- make a regulation for granting a rebate on damaged -tobacco. That i-s the point I make.
I have no particular interest in the subject because my province does not grow tobacco, but (I -submit -that the minister is not authorized by subsection 6 to make such a regulation as he suggests can be made.
I am advised by the officials of the department that the Inland Revenue Act contains a section which, beyond doubt, gives power to the department to frame regulations covering that point.
If -there is some other provision, all right.

The tax of five cents a pound to be imposed under subsection 3 of section 328A is a general tax. Now I am raising tobacco, which I sell for fifteen or twenty cents a pound, and my neighbour raises a higher quality of tobacco for which he receives thirty-five cents a pound, it is not fair that I should be called -upon to pay the same amount of tax as he does. There should be a distinction made, and in my opinion it would be -more just to base the tax upon the value of the tobacco. The Quesnel tobaco raised in the county of Montcalm -brings thirty-five or forty cents a pound, whereas Blue Briar, or Comstock fetches much less. There should be a difference in the scale of taxation based on the selling price. I drew the minister's attention to that fact.
I am instructed that there is no country in the world where there is an ad valorem duty on tobacco. I do not -quite see how you could impose taxation of that kind.
What about cigars?
The duty is specific. I do not see how you could fix a rate of duty upon the selling price.
In the Customs Department you have gaugers who test the wines and liquors. Could you not have experts to determine the quality of tobacco?
I am afraid we would have to have tobacco tasters. [DOT]
My hon. friend knows there are tobacco expertsvall over the country.

I suppose the
manufacturer has persons to determine values.

There are experts in
the United States also.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) raises an inferior quality of tobacco on which he pays so much a pound. Perhaps he raises more of that inferior quality than his neighbour.
No.
If not, why does not the hon. gentleman take a leaf out of his neighbour's 'book and go in for growing tobacco of better quality, which will realize a higher price.
The reason I am not raising tobacco of better quality than my neighbour is because the soil is not the same. His soil will produce Quesnel tobacco, mine will not.

That is a fair
answer.
Therefore I have to raise another quality of tobacco.

I do not think that anybody can complain of this tax upon Canadian grown leaf tobacco. It is a very email excise tax indeed, and I think there will be no complaint. The producer of the Canadian leaf enjoys very high protection, and it is only fair that he should pay something in the nature of an excise tax.

We do not complain of the. tax of five cents. We have been fairly treated in this instance by the Government, and I tender them my best thanks on that account. But is it just that I should be required to pay the same tax as my immediate neighbour, who produces a much superior quality, and gets a higher price for it? It is generally recognized that there 
must be some sacrifice, and that the duty of five cents a pound is a fair one, but there should foe a distinction made in the rate of duty paid as between the man who realizes thirty-five or forty cents a pound on his tobacco, and the man whose tobacco only brings him in from fifteen to twenty cents a pound.

Tobaccos are graded into
classes 1, 2 and' 3, so it can be easily determined by any one making an adjustment what amount of tax different sections of the country should ibe required to pay. A6 to one farmer having a better crop than another, to which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) referred, let me draw his attention to the trouble that is experienced' on account of frost. Frost may be experienced in one particular section, and half a mile away there may be no frost. One man's crop of tobacco may be seriously affected toy frost, whereas another man's crop may not receive any damage at all from that cause.
(That is where the injustice would come in. It would not be the fault of the owuer, but that his crop happened to be damaged on account of the peculiar situation of the land or the quality of the soil, which might attract frost -more quickly than would other sections close to the water or to the lake in my district, and whose crops would not be damaged by frost, while those further inland would be. It is no reflection on the farmer who has his tobacco frosted so far as his ability as a farmer is concerned,, but it is due to where he is situated. If the acting minister will give us some assurance that his regulation will cover such cases I feel satisfied that it will be some encouragement to producers to go into the tobacco industry.
Mr. DuTREMiBLAY:	I drew the attention of the acting minister the other day to the effect of the tax on tobacco. I asked if the tax of 5 cents per pound- was to be paid by the manufacturers of cigars, and I understood 'the minister to reply that it was. The manufacturers already pay an excise tax of 20 cents a pound, and if they have to pay the additional 5 cents they will be taxed 25 cents a pound.

In answer to what the hon. gentleman has just said, I am in principle opposed to the tax of 5 cents upon farmers who grow tobacco. I remember when the tax of 28 cents per pound was imposed on foreign raw leaf tobacco that the eastern and western tobacco growers sent a very important delegation to the Capital asking for a further duty of 10 cents a pound on American leaf to protect the Canadian growers. We discussed the matter with the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), and the Minister of the Interior, and they were convinced at that time that an additional duty of 10 cents was necessary to protect the Canadian grower. We left the Capital fully satisfied that we had made, our point, but on the following day the cigar manufacturers came to Ottawa and did their utmost to induce the Government not to impose the tax of 10 cents that we were asking. Our contention then, as to-dav, wTas that the 28 cents per pound tax
on American tobacco was not sufficient. But in the new tariff the Government has raised the excise on American tobacco from 28 cents up to 40 and to 60 cents per pound. That leaves a margin of 12 cents in our favour, and we are only called upon to pay a tax of 5 cents. The difference between 12 and 5 cents is 7 cents, therefore the tobacco growers have an advantage now in their favour of 7 cents. It being admitted that all must do their duty, I am satisfied that the 5 cent tax should be imposed upon Canadian tobacco growers, because there is now a very large difference in our favour. That is why I do not oppose the new tax of 5 cents, because really we now have 35 oents per pound protection against American tobacco, and our growers are able to compete with it. Of course, it would be better still if we had no tax to pay at all, but everybody must bear his share of taxation at this time.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the Bill?

Before you report the Bill, Mr. Chairman, I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of 'Customs to the fact that complaint has been .made in various parts of the county from which I come that since the importation of liquor has been prohibited the Department of Customs has not taken much interest in the protection of the community generally with regard to the manufacture of liquors in illicit stills. It is said that officers of the department have been withdrawn, that these liquors are being illegally manufactured and sold in a great many places1 and that considerable damage and disturbance is resulting. I am sure that the minister will not be less vigilant in suppressing this illegal manufacture simply because its suppression will not bring any money into the coffers of the country. Active steps should be taken to suppress this evil. Complaints also come to me from my own county and from other parts of Eastern Canada about the indiscriminate granting of customs warehouse licenses to people who have liquors. No man who is engaged directly or indirectly in the sale of liquors should be given a license to store liquors on his premises. No matter how innocent he may be, the temptation thereby put in his way is extraordinary and should not exist. I have no personal knowledge of it, but I understand that a great many licenses have heen granted within the last two months to persons in eastern Nova Scotia who are engaged in the sale of liquor. I have not

closely followed the different Orders in Council which have heen passed-

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue; Minister of Customs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer [DOT]to persons engaged in the legal sale of liquor under license from the Provincial Government?
No liquor is legally sold in the province except by a few vendors who are specially appointed in different places.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue; Minister of Customs
speechtext: My hon. friend does not refer to these vendors?

No. There is only one vendor in the Island of Cape Breton-I know him .personally-and he has no warehouse. But a great many of these warehouses in eastern Nova Scotia have been stored largely with liquors within the last few weeks. A good deal of agitation prevails among the people of eastern Nova Scotia on this account. I have not the reputation of being much of a temperance man-

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue; Minister of Customs
speechtext: I am sorry to hear it.

-although I may be a temperance man in a general way. But this Government should do everything in their power to co-operate with local governments in enforcing the law. When a local Legislature and the local Government has done everything possible to stop the sale of liquor, no assistance to the contrary should be given by any department of this Government.

I am afraid the minister has not given sufficient consideration to the objection made to subsection (c) of 279 regarding the tax on cigars. It is provided that the tax on cigars of all descriptions made from raw leaf tobacco or .any substitute therefor shall be $6 per thousand. It is not reasonable that all cigars should be included in the same class. I have no expert knowledge of the matter, but I assume that all cigars are manufactured from r.aw leaf tobacco either imported or grown in the country. The price of cigars varies from 5 cents to $1 each. I never smoke the $1 cigars, but I have no doubt that some hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite do so. The tax on these $1 cigars is just the same as the tax on the poor man's cigar, which sells at 5 cents or even less. Unless the minister amends this clause, I wish to enter my protest against its being past in its present form.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue; Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The matter mentioned by the member for North Cape Breton and

Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has already come to the attention of the Government through telegrams from the temperance associations and other organizations in Nova Scotia. Attention has been given to it, and a telegram recently received from the mayor of Sydney stated that the regulations now being carried out are entirely satisfactory. Instructions were immediately given that no liquor of any kind or description should be removed from an Inland Revenue bonded warehouse or a Customs warehouse in Nova Scotia except for export purposes under the supervision of an officer of the department; and it was pointed out that if these instructions w'ere not observed, a change would be made of .all the officials in Nova Scotia.

I have already given consideration to representations similar to those which have just been made by the member for Antigonish and Guysbor-ough (Mr. Sinclair).
In order to impose upon tobaccos an excise tax according to the selling price, it would be necessary to revise all our excise resolutions upon cigars and tobaccos. That principle has never been adopted in this country, and I do not deem it wise, at least at the present time, to introduce any such change. The tax upon cigars, as I have already stated this morning, amounts to two-thirds of a cent for each cigar.
My point is that it should be an ad valorem tax in place of a specific tax..

I do not .see how you could have an ad valorem duty upon tobaccos. You might have a specific duty upon the selling price.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: In the United States there is a specific duty" upon quality, not upon quantity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the Bill is reported, I wish to draw the attention of hon. -members to the fact that the motion to report a Bill is not debatable, and, therefore, the final debate which has just taken place has, as I understand it, taken place with the unanimous consent of the committee. I do not wish it to be taken as a precedent, because hon. members, on reading rule 17 (a), will see that while the preamble or the title of a Bill is debatable, a motion that the committee rise and report is not debatable.	.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On section 1-tax on berths and parlour car seats increased:
How are these amounts collected by the Government?
From the Tailways.
Monthly?
Quarterly.
What revenue was derived last year?

I would direct the attention of the acting minister to a mistake which, I think, underlies all these specific taxes. There is, for instance, no attempt made 'by this tax of ten cents for a chair in a parlour car to differentiate between the man who travels twenty-five miles and the man who sits in the car all day and travels three- hundred miles. They each pay ten cents. There should be some difference. The difference between five and ten cents seems trivial; but the principle is something, and it would be well to start right in regard to these taxes, because I do not contemplate the removal of any of these taxes for many years to -come. This kind of taxation will have to -exist for years, and it should be started on a just and fair basis. It is neither just nor fair to charge one man ten cents for travelling 25 miles in a parlour car and another man ten cents for travelling 300 miles in a parlour car.
Section agreed to
On section 2-proprietary and patent medicines:

I should -like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which has been the cause of a good deal of trouble and confusion amongst the manufacturers of a certain line of medicines -and the medical profession of the country. I feel that those who drafted the original Act which was passed in 1915, were not very familiar with the drug business. There is a line of preparations which are very largely manufactured to-day and which do not strictly come under the definition of proprietary or patent medicines. They are not patent medicines; they are not strictly speaking, proprietary medicines, but they are termed pharmaceuticals-
Are they mentioned in the pharmacopoeias?

They are preparations made by the manufacturers for the convenience 0-f the physici-ans. The old style of preparing medicines in the doctor's office, using the crude drugs, and preparing them and the noxious mixtures that most of us received when we were younger, has largely passed away, and the preparation of medicines is now largely in the hands of those manufacturers who -prepare them under the term " pharmaceutical preparations." They prepare them under -scientific methods, and they have succeeded in presenting preparations which are fairly palatable, yet using just the drugs -that would -be used by the	doctors if	they were following the old method of preparation.
This is -a development for the convenience of the medical profession. The medicine iis put up in pound lots, half-gallon, gallon, or five-gallon lots, according to the requirements of tihe -individual physician. It was generally understood for a time after the passing of the Act in 1915 that these did not come under that Act, and many manufacturers sold them under the impression that they were not included. I might add that on the labels of these preparations the dose and the purpose of the medicine is generally shown. 1-t was held by the department that the fact o-f the dose and the purpose of the medicine being given brought the medicines under the Act. There is no quarrel on the part of the manufacturers or the physicians as to the payment of taxes. What they desire is a clear understanding on this point so that the confusion which has hitherto existed m-ay be removed. An effort has been made in the

Bill now before the House to correct that to some extent, but even now I do not think it is going to make it very clear. For instance, the new definition of consumer is, "*Consumer means any person who uses or purchases." Now, this difficulty will arise. The physician purchases from the manufacturer and therefore, as I understand it, he will be a consumer and will have to pay the tax as he prescribes these medicines. He may fill an eight-ounce bottle from a half-gallon jar and1 give it to the patient; the patient then becomes the consumer and the user, and will also be liable to a tax on the same preparation. If my impression is not correct I should be 'glad to hear from the minister. Paragraph 2 does not make clear the point which has caused confusion in the past. It ' says:
Any preparation manufactured for sale exclusively for the medical profession and on the labels of which no claim is made that the preparation has medicinal or curative powers or any directions with respect to the amount that constitutes a proper dose.
It is almost necessary for the manufacturer to put the dose on tlhe label. It is also very convenient -for the label to state whether the remedy ils a diuretic or stomachic, telling what the preparation is useful for. If the words " intelligible to the public " were inserted after " claim " it might remove tlhe difficulty which has .arisen in the past and which I feel will arise under the Bill as now drafted. I only desire to clear up the confusion. The physicians of Ontario have been bothered a good deal by inspectors coming around and taking samples of medicines from their offices which the physicians considered exempt from the tax. This confusion exposed the physicians to the danger of being fined $50 and costs for violation of the law I merely draw these matters to the attention of the .minister, hoping that some change may be made to clarify the whole matter and relieve the manufacturers and the physicians from the dangers to which they were exposed under the old law.

I believe the whole
tax on patent medicines is wrong. I happen to know something about the drug business, and 1 think it is a shame to make the consumer pay the tax. I should like to know how much revenue has been obtained from this source during the last year.

The manufacturer

speechtext: When the committee rose at one o'clock we were considering Bill No. 83 to amend the Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and clause 1 had been adopted. Clause 2 had been read and was being discussed. Shall clause 2 carry?

As hon. gentlemen are aware, it is the consumer who will ultimately pay this tax, and he is the one who has to pay always. I suggest that the Acting Minister of Finance reconsider the form in which this tax has been proposed before it goes into operation, that instead of four per cent the tax he made one per cent and that the manufacturer be required to pay it. It is the manufacturer we should endeavour to reach because he makes the largest profits. At present there is an army of men going round the country endeavouring to find out whether "pain-killer and other preparations are properly stamped, and these men are entailing an expenditure to the public of about $96,000. Now that prohibition is in force I think we should endeavour to save this big amount. The Acting Minister of Finance, who used to be so straightforward and fair in his criticism of taxation when he sat on this side of the House, is, I am afraid, learning had tricks and instead of getting after the manufacturer seems to want to protect the big interests. The manufacturer should be made to shell out a little money; should be made to pay his ishaTe of taxation and not let the burden fall upon the consumer. I make that suggestion to my, hon. friend because I think it is a fair one.

From the standpoint of administration my hon. friend (Mr. Fournier) is perfectly correct, and in the
preparation of the amendments to the Special War Revenue Act I was personally very much impressed with the same view. I want to assure imy hon. friend that I tried in every possible way to devise amendments to the Act along the lines which he suggests, but I was unable to do so. It would be infinitely cheaper to collect the tax from the importer and the manufacturer, but there were difficulties in the way, such as I pointed out this morning and I could not see any way of overcoming them. It is unfortunate that we are unable to determine exactly the amount of revenue which will be derived from this particular source. That is largely due to the fact that the Special War Revenue Act, when first introduced, was amended upon the suggestion of Parliament to permit the use of postage stamps as well as inland revenue stamps. It is quite possible to devise a particular stamp to be used in the sales of drugs, but it would be very inconvenient to the public at many points. It is not always easy to obtain inland revenue stamps, whereas in all sections of the country postage stamps are available to the public. It was in the interest of the public generally that the amendment was made at the time of the introduction of the Bill in 1915, and permission given to use postage stamps as well as inland revenue stamps, but I think that now it will be inconvenient to the public to restore the Bill to its original form in so far as this particular point is concerned.

On section 3

tax on matches and playing cards:

I rise again to draw the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance to the way in which this tax of eight cents on playing cards will work out to the prejudice of the poor. Now the people who are accustomed to buy inexpensive cards, and can afford none other, at from fifteen to twenty cents a package, will find they will be paying a tax of about fifty per cent, while those who buy more expensive play-ipg cards will escape with a comparatively light tax. This is a matter as to which I may tire the ears of the minister, but he may hear me on account of my importunity, as in the case of the widow in the Scriptures. I do press very strongly upon the Government the advisability of placing these small taxes-these small direct taxes -on an equitable basis, in which the ad valorem principle will einteT. The answer may be that these are only



trifling taxes, that they amount to very little in. each individual ease. I grant it is a small tax, but if we are going to have a large number of these taxes, in the aggregate they will amount to something, and should be baked on the principle of justice. I am sure the Government of this country would not wish those blessed with a very small portion of this worlds goods to have a feeling of injustice against the Government, and I fear that feeling may he created if a large number of these small taxes are imposed which will operate to the disadvantage of the poor as compared with the rich. And where you have such a tax as is found in this section,-of eight cents a pack on playing cards, that is a heavy tax on a cheap pack of cards and it is a light tax on an expensive pack.
Mr. A. K. MAlCJLEAN: You can lose the same amount of money with a cheap pack as with an expensive one.

The Acting Finance
Minister is wrong. The man earning fifteen dollars a week is unable to lose as much money on cards for which he has paid but a small amount, and which will be required to pay eight cents tax, as the man of large means.
Oh, oh.

Of course, the acting minister means that as a joke. We all understand that. But I am not joking; I am perfectly serious, in bringing this matter before the House, that these specific taxes work out unjustly, and an attempt should be made by the Government to place these small taxes on an ad valorem basis, so that the people will be taxed in proportion to their means. That is the principle on which even these smaller taxes should be based.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It seems desirable in connection with this Bill to make a statement of a more or less general nature with regard to the whole railway situation in Canada at the present time, and especially as- it has developed during the past fifteen years.
I need not do more than refer to the proposals brought down by the Government of the day in 1903, and amended by a subsequent Act in 1904, under which the National Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific have been constructed. At that time the Canadian Northern railway had attained considerable development in the Prafrie Provinces, and had begun to feel the necessity of some connection with the East, or some expansion in the East, in order that it might gather up eastern traffic for its western lines, and in order that its western traffic might be transferred to lines in the East which it owned or with which it had connections.
It seems beyond question-and I am not saying this by way of criticism-that if an arrangement at that time could have been consummated between the Grand Trunk railway in the East and the Canadian Northern lines in the West, if they could have been connected by a new railway passing north of lake Superior, the combined railway system thus created would have been in a splendid position to-day. During the past four or five years it would, if it were necessary, have been able to lend money to Canada instead of coming, both in the East and in the West, to Parliament year after year for the purpose of obtaining such aid as would prevent these roads from going into liquidation. However, that course was not adopted. Possibly on account of the conflicting views of those who were entrusted with the management of those two railway systems, it may have been impossible to adopt it. As to that I do not know.
The project of the National Transcontinental railway, including the Grand Trunk Pacific, proceeded after the legislation of 1903 and 1904, and shortly afterwards the

Government of the day extended to the Canadian Northern railway such aid as was designed to enable it to have the desired connection in Eastern Canada. By chapter 11 of the Act of 1908, a guarantee of bonds by this country to the Canadian Northern railway was authorized at the rate of $13,000 per mile in respect of 609 miles of railway in the Prairie Provinces. By chapter 6 of the Acts of 1910, Parliament authorized the guarantee of bonds for 150 miles to be constructed by the Canadian Northern Alberta Company, 50 miles at $13,000 per mile, and the remainder at $25,000 per mile. By chapter 6 of the Acts of 1911, Parliament authorized a guarantee of bonds for the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company at the rate of $35,000 per mile for 1,050 miles, which were to connect the western lines of the Canadian Northern railway with the lines which it had acquired in the East.
There was a new Administration in 1911. Very shortly after that Administration had been formed, it became abundantly evident, not only to Parliament but to the people of this.country, that neither one nor the other of these two undertakings could be carried to completion unless the country granted further aid.
The Government had then to decide whether these railways should be permitted to go into liquidation, with all the consequent confusion and apprehended1 detriment to the public interest, or whether the Government and Parliament should evidence strong confidence in the future . ability of the. country to 'sustain those railways when completed. After very careful and anxious consideration, it was determined to give such aid as would enable the two undertakings to be carried to a conclusion. In 1912 and 1913 certain aid was given to the Canadian Northern Railway company, and in 1913 and in 1914 certain aid was granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company. I shall, however, at a later date, go more in detail into the aid afforded to the latter railway.
By chapter 7 of the Acts of 1912 the Canadian Northern Railway company was gj-anted a guarantee of bonds at $35,000 pel mile for 115 miles. By chapter 10 of the Acts of 1913 a subsidy was granted on 250 miles from Toronto to Ottawa at $6,400 per mile, on 910 miles from Ottawa to Port Arthur at $12,000 per mile, and on 260 miles from Edmonton to the British Columbia boundary at $12,000 -per mile. In consideration of the subsidies so granted the Canadian Northern Railway company was
126i
called upon by .the terms of the statute to transfer $7,000,000 of its capital stock to the Government. By -chapter 20 of the Acts of 1914, founded upon evidence presented to Parliament of the inability of the Canadian Northern Railway system to complete its undertaking without a further guarantee of bonds, it was provided that a guarantee of $45,000,000 should be made, in consideration of which $33,000,000 of -the capital istncK ot tne company was to be transferred to -the people. The capital stock at that -time was increased to $100,000,000, and the net result of the transaction, apart-from the guarantee itself, was that for the future the former proprietors of the railway were to own $60,000,000 of the stock and the people of Canada $40,000,000.
I expressed the opinion at that -time-and I think my colleagues concurred in it- that under ordinary conditions that guarantee of bonds would enable the Canadian Northern Railway company to complete its system, and that there would be no further application to Parliament for assistance. But the war broke out in the beginning of Augus-t, 1914, and it became apparent in the following two or three years that the Canadian Northern and- the Grand Trunk Pacific would require further assistance if they were not ,to be forced in liquidation. We had before us the same consideration as that previously presented to us, and, taking into account all the elements entering into the situation at that time, we reached the conclusion that the road should be sustained; that there should1 not be liquidation. Ultimately, that view-which, if 1 remember correctly, was shared on both sides -of the House-was confirmed by the report of the commission of inquiry, to which I shall call attention later. So by chapter 4 Of the Acts of 1915 a loan of $10,000,000 was made to the -Canadian Northern Railway Company and by the Appropriation Act No. 2, page 36 of the s-tatutes of 1916, a further loan of $15,000,000 was made to the same company, a total of $25,000,000.
The conditions induced by the war; the very greatly increased cost of fuel, material, and labour; the consequent falling off of net earnings; the inability to market securities which had been guaranteed' by the Parliament of Canada and by provincial Legislatures, made it impossible for the Canadian Northern Railway Company to complete its undertaking, and to meet its fixed charges, even with the assistance to which I have referred. Consequently, -at the last session of Parliament, we were once more faced with the problem in respect to

in that regard. I have conferred with those who have been present at the arbitration; I know what has been communicated to us by counsel in charge of the case on behalf of the Government, and I desire to assure not only the hon. member for Russell but every hon. member of this House that there has been the fullest and most absolute freedom to the Government of this country to have all information of every .kind respecting that road, its properties, its assets, its earnings and its liabilities, that could have been afforded under any circumstances whatever. As a matter of fact I am told that the information prepared by those who were the proprietors of the Canadian Northern railway until the stock was vested in the Government has been submitted to counsel for the Government even before it was presented to the arbitrators.

speechtext: I do not like to interrupt, buf; I hold in my hand a newspaper item giving effect to a complaint from Mr. Tilley that he .had not received information.

speechtext:
X am informed by an officer who was present at the arbitration that that particular complaint was made by reason of the fact that the infor- -mation which had been asked for required considerable time to prepare; it was on its way to Mr. Tilley .at the time he made the complaint, and it has been received by him in due course.
The time for making the award was originally limited to the first day of March last. It has since been extended, I think, on two occasions, and it is now extended io the first day of June. It is believed that the argument will be completed and the award made before that date shall have expired.
In the meantime the management of the Canadian Northern Railway has been left undisturbed to this extent. Three men nominated by the Government' have been appointed to the board of the Canadian Northern Railway. They have been elected as directors of the road and have the fullest possible access to the proceedings of the directors and take part in their proceedings, and without their knowledge nothing can be done by the board of management of the railway. The reason for leaving the management undisturbed in this way until after the award has been made .is that the Government has in the meantime absolutely full and complete access to all the documents and records of the company, and every opportunity for
ISir Robert Borden.]
necessary information has been available to the officers and counsel of the Government. That being so, it was not considered desirable that during the progress of the arbitration the Government should make itself responsible for the management of the railway; the reasons for this will, I think, occur to any hon,. gentleman in this House upon reflection. Until the arbitration had reached a conclusion it would be desirable that the management of the company, as heretofore existing, should be held responsible for the condition and operation of the road during the period of investigation. There was no advantage in changing the management in the meantime, as all the books, documents and records of the company were fully available. Moreover, it was considered, and this conclusion was reached after very careful consideration, that >any change made in the meantime might demoralize the staff, and that a permanent change ought not to be made until the Government would be in a position to make a permanent arrangement with the staff. On many occasions during the past six or eight months we have had deputations from the railway organizations of this country, representing the employees not only of the Canadian Northern, but of all the railways of this country. Representations have been made by these delegations to the Government as to the conditions under which that road ought to be carried on and operated by the Government, as to the continuity of e'ertain arrangements made between the Canadian Northern Railway and its employees in the past, as to provision for pensions and the continuance of the arrangements already made in that regard. Various matters of this kind have been taken up and on the whole it was thought desirable that the Government should not make itself directly responsible for the management and operation of the road by appointing an absolutely new board of directors until after the -award had been made and the proposals in that regard carried out. I cannot better express the view of the Government as entertained at the last -session of Parliament than by quoting the words of the Minister of Finance on the first day of August, 1917, as follows;
As to the Board we shall have to get in the stock first and complete the transaction, and then it will be open to the Board to determine what is the best course, having regard to the public interest, to pursue with regard to the

board of Directors and the general administration of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
It is proper, however, to observe, as this question seems to have excited .some interest in the minds of hon. members on both sides of the House, that it is not intended that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann shall be members of the board as reconstituted. As a matter of fact, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann have expressed their desire to be relieved from further responsibility with respect to this railway after it passes into the hands of the Government, and after the amount of the award, whatever it may be, shall have been determined. They have also said, Sir William Mackenzie in particular has said, that he is very intimately acquainted with the development of the road, with its operation and everything [DOT]connected with it from the very first, and if at any time he can be of any service to the board of directors without remuneration or compensation by giving advice or otherwise, he will be very happy to make his services available to them in any way that they may determine.
Now with regard to the operating of the road. Hon. gentlemen of this House will understand that this is a very large question indeed. On more than one occasion in the past I have spoken of the difficulties which confront a Government after the capital stock of a great railway enterprise ' such as this has passed into the ownership of the people of Canada. I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, and I know we all have a common purpose in this, will agree that a great railway system such as that which is now being acquired ought not to be administered directly by any department of the Government.
I think we may start with that.
Another proposition which undoubtedly will be accepted by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House is this. While a road under the ownership of the people of Canada must be subject to the direction and control of the people in the highest sense, in the larger political sense; nevertheless, it is absolutely essential and vital that political influence in the lower sense-party political influence-shall be completely absent from the administration and operation of the road. These are two perfectly sound propositions. It is easy to lay down such propositions, accepted on both sides of this House, but it is a somewhat different problem to devise a scheme by which those two desiderata can be absolutely secured in the future operation of the State railways
of Canada. That is the problem with which this Government has been confronted and with which it is now confronted. That is the problem which this Government and this Parliament must solve .at the earliest possible .moment. The problem is not concerned with the Canadian Northern railway alone. It is concerned also with the	Intercolonial	Railway,	with the
Transcontinental Railway, and, more than that, it is extremely likely that, in the not distant future, it will be concerned with the Grand Trunk Pacific and with the Grand Trunk Railway itself. Thus, it is a very comprehensive problem in its scope and it is. exceedingly difficult for the Government and Parliament to find an adequate solution.
As to the immediate future, I have already said that we do not intend to operate the Canadian Northern Railway system directly under a department o.f the Government; it is our intention to operate it for the present through the corporate machinery by which it has been operated in the past. There will he a reconstituted hoard of directors. We shall endeavour to get the best men we can and we shall not interfere with them. We shall leave the administration and operation of that road to be carried on absolutely under that board of directors and we shall use every means available to the Government (and if necessary, we shall come to Parliament for that purpose) in order that anything like political influence, political patronage, or political interference-I am using the word political in its narrower sense-shall be absolutely eliminated from the administration of that road.
But, more than that, we have under consideration the .question as to whether it may not be possible in the immediate future to bring the Transcontinental Railway, which is the property of the people of Canada, and the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways, which are also the property of the people of Canada, under corporate management. I do not desire to commit the Government to what I am mentioning just now, because we have had no opportunity in the very great stress and hurry of this session to give the proposition mature consideration. It may he possible, and, more than that, it may be desirable, to bring the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways under the ownership of the corporation which will control the Canadian Northern. The people of Canada will own absolutely the entire stock of the Canadian Northern

Railway system. If the Transcontinental railway, the Intercolonial railway and the Prince Edward Island railway were amalgamated into one system with the Canadian Northern railway and were operated with it as one system and under one corporate management, it might, and doubtless would be, very greatly in the interest of efficient administration and operation. That suggestion is before the Government. It is a suggestion upon which I invite an expression of opinion from hon. gentlemen in this House. As far as- I have 'been able to give it consideration, it commends itself very much to my judgment.
Now, I come to speak of some matters upon which my right hon, friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) desired information in connection with the Canadian Northern railway. I shall go into that first, and afterwards I shall have to say something about the financial position of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. But just one word before I deal with that.
_ It is only right to explain that conditions in regard to railway operation, expenditure and income which have prevailed in Canada since this war and which have necessitated frequent applications for aid by the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific are to-day finding their parallel in some portions of the United States. The Pennsylvania Railway system in the United States is one of the greatest railway systems in the world. Under ordinary conditions it has a net revenue over operating expenses of from $50,000,000 to $64,000,000.
I have learned from authoritative sources that during the month of January last the Pennsylvania Railway system failed to meet its operating expenses by $2,816,900.76, and that in the month of February last it failed to meet its operating expenses by $3,354,258.56.

With added interest it would, of course, run to at least $100,000 per mile. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway consists of the Mountain Section from Prince Rupert to Wolf Creek, 833 miles, and the Prairie Section from Wolf Creek to Winnipeg, 915 miles, a total of 1,748 miles. I have under my hand a statement of the expenditure upon the road itself and for rolling stock. The last available, that of Sir Collimgwood Schreiber, is $135,698,615.64, but that does not include equipment and rolling stock. If you add what has been expended for equipment and rolling stock, you will find that it brings the expenditure for construction and for equipment and rolling stock (which I have included in the liabilities of the Canadian Northern) up to about $180,000,000, a capitalization for the Grand Trunk Pacific of $100,000 per mile, instead of $44,000 or $45,000 per mile, the capitalization for the Canadian Northern railway.

Without interest, it works out to $92,000 per mile, and with interest it would work out, the financial comptroller tells me, at about $110,000 per mile. I thought it desirable to give these comparisons to the House and to the country in order that they might realize that we are not buying a pig in a poke in acquiring the Canadian Northern railway, and that, so far as property owned by the State is concerned, the future holds out greater prospects for the Canadian Northern Railway system than for any other railway that is to-day within the control and dis-'position of the Government of Canada.
I come now to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I regard it as inevitable that, for many reasons, that road should Ibe taken over by the Federal Government. It is a national enterprise to which the credit of the Canadian people has been committed, and, in my judgment, it is expedient.to sustain it and not permit it to go into liquidation. It is intimately connected with the Grand Trunk Railway system in the East. The Canadian Northern branch lines in the West can, in many instances, as I am informed, be made available as feeders for the Grand Trunk Pacific without great expenditure. The road, as it is at present, is not self-sustaining. It pays a little more than operating expenses, although I am hound to .say that, during the past eight or twelve months, it has rather exceeded anticipations in the return which it has made. The House and the country will he glad to know that the prospects of its traffic seem to he improving, and I very sincerely hope that they will improve still more in the early future. That railway cannot be successfully operated without suitable arrangements with the Canadian Northern Railway and with the Grand Trunk-Railway in the East. It cannot pay its interest charges, and it is utterly impossible for the Grand Trunk to meet the obligations which it has undertaken in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. That has been publicly stated. It is stated in the Drayton-Acworth report. Therefore, as the Grand Trunk Pacific is not self-sustaining, as it pays little more than operating expenses, and as it cannot be expected, for many years to come, to pay its fixed charges, especially if it is divorced from co-operation and association with other railways in the West, it is manifest that only one 
of two courses is open. The Government must either year after year ask Parliament to vote seven or eight or ten million dollars in order that the fixed charges of the road may be paid, or it must take over the road, connect it up as effectively as possible with the Canadian Northern and with the rest of the Government railway system, and endeavour to make it part of a profitable system of Government railways in the early future. I think, therefore, it is absolutely inevitable that the Grand Trunk Pacific must be acquired. As to the terms of its acquisition, I can only say that the Grand Trunk would no doubt be willing to hand it over to us today if we would relieve the Grand Trunk of all its obligations in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific; it would hand over to us the capital stock and he glad to get out of its own obligations in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific. But there are several conditions to ibe taken into account before any such proposal can be entertained, and so we are at the present time discussing the whole situation with the Grand Trunk management. As an additional reason, which I did not previously mention, if we permitted the Grand Trunk Pacific to go into liquidation, we should have to take care of all those obligations which are prior to our own, and that would in the end mean that we would simply have to take care of all the obligations of that railway. Thus, there is no object whatever in permitting it to go into liquidation. It would merely mean additional expense, dislocation of traffic and the exciting of public alarm, without any good result that I can anticipate.
Now it seems if we tdke over the Grand Trunk Pacific, that practically involves the taking over of the Grand Trunk Railway as well. I am of that opinion for this chief reason, that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, both in the West, if acquired by the Government would otherwise lack eastern connections, and the Canadian Pacific Railway would dominate the whole situation. In the second place, the Grand Trunk might have a great deal of difficulty in carrying on unless it should be released from its obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Further than that, while the present condition of the Grand Trunk is not prosperous for many reasons, some of which doubtless it could not control, I believe that it would have reasonable -prospects for the future if amalgamated into one system with the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. I would further emphasize the consideration that,

while the Grand Trunk cannot carry out the obligations necessary for its retention of the Grand Trunk Pacific, on the other hand it has no bright future prospects without that connection. Hon. members of this House who recollect the report of Mr. Hays, upon which the National Transcontinental enterprise was largely founded, will remember that he pointed out the anomalous situation in which the Grand Trunk found itself. It gathered up traffic all over Eastern Canada and handed it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway, which earned very large carrying charges for transporting that traffic to the West. The same condition would confront the Grand Trunk to-day unless it had that western connection to which Mr. Hays, then general manager of the . Grand Trunk Railway, looked forward with so much anticipation of good results.
It is very easy to say that this country ought to acquire the Grand Trunk Railway, but when one comes down to the practical proposal of how it is to be acquired the problem is not quite so simple. Of course we might take advantage of a situation which to some extent has developed out of the disturbed conditions of the world, and say to the management of the Grand Trunk Railway, "We have you in our power in certain respects, and you must do precisely what we insist upon." But on the other hand, we must remember not only in this connection but in many other connections, that Canada is a country which for many years to come will require to borrow large amounts of capital from other countries. If the Federal Government or any provincial government in Canada lays itself open to the reasonable charge of acting unfairly or unjustly towards those who in good faith have invested their capital in business enterprises of this character in Canada, the country in the end will pay much more than it will gain by any sucn injustice; there is absolutely no doubt about that in my mind. So we must acj^ reasonably with the Grand Trunk railway, and we have endeavoured to act reasonably with them. But more than that, if we undertake to force the situation against the Grand Trunk railway, we must also remember that a considerable portion of that system lies in the United States, with two great terminals in the West, I believe, and one great terminal in the East. The ownership of these lines is vested in United States companies, of which the Grand Trunk controls the stock, and that makes their acquisition even with the consent of the Grand Trunk railway, a matter of no little difficulty and
complexity. So I think the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway must depend upon negotiation. We could, of course, cut these lines off at the border and expropriate them, dislocating the system; but we would do ourselves no good and the Grand Trunk railway irreparable harm by attempting such a course.
I may say that we have negotiations outstanding with the Grand Trunk railway. For the present they are confidential. We have made what we regard as a reasonable offer, somewhat along the lines suggested in the Drayton-Acworth report, but somewhat more favourable to the Grand Trunk than the proposal made in that report. They have replied to us by making a counter offer, which was of such a nature that we did not consider we could ask Parliament to accept it. For that reason we had to decline it, and we then made the suggestion to the management that, failing any agreement between the Government and the company, we would be prepared to submit the amount of the annual payment to arbitration, and we would do that without fixing any limit as we did in the case of the Canadian Northern railway. It seemed to us that the two cases were distinguishable in that respect, and that we ought not to insist upon a maximum as we did in the case of the Canadian Northern. We proposed to follow the Drayton-Acworth report in this respect, that whatever sum should be paid by the Government of this country for, let us say, a lease of the Grand Trunk Railway lines, should be distributed among the holders of the various stocks of the Grand Trunk Pacific by the directors of the Grand Trunk themselves, and that we should not attempt to interfere with or control that matter. It is anticipated that some members of the Government will have the duty of proceeding to Great Britain during this summer. A sub-committee of Council has been appointed, and during the past six months has been dealing with general railway problems in this country, assisting in that regard the Minister of Railways and Canals, who is primarily responsible, and who had asked me to have such a sub-committee appointed in order that he might, without a formal meeting of Council, have the advice of some of his colleagues in respect of matters of importance. Two members of that sub-committee of Council will be in England during the summer. They have given attentive study to the questions which are involved, and I have some reasonable hope that when Parliament its again summoned, the Govern-

ment may be in a position to place before it proposals which will involve the constitution into one State-owned system, the chief railways of Canada, except the Canadian Pacific. It may be possible, indeed I think it is probable, that at some later date, but not in the immediate future, all the land transportation facilities of Canada in the shape of railways may, so far as operation is concerned, be amalgamated into one system carried on under one management. The enormous waste and duplication, which have proved to be such a burden upon this country in the past, would be eliminated, for the future at least, in that way; and they have been eliminated to some extent during the past six or eight months as I shall demonstrate by a report which I propose to read before I sit Mown.
I should also say to the members of the House, before I leave that branch of the subject, that the Government have not been unmindiful of their duty to see that adequate rolling stock and motive power should be provided for all the railways of Canada as far as possible during the past twelve or fifteen months. The Department of Railways and 'Canals, during that time, assisted the Grand Trunk in the matter of motive power to a very considerable extent. They provided for them 47 Mikado engines. 'The department has at the present time under order for the Grand Trunk railway 75 Mikado engines, 20 switching engines and 15 Pacific type passenger engines. The 47 Mikado engines which we secured .at $48,750 each were ordered about six months before the 75 Mikado engines which are to cost us $62,000 each. It is necessary to have these engines to keep the railway systems of the country up to their full power for transportation purposes, [DOT] and while providing- very amply for the railways under the direct control and administration of the department, we have also found it necessary to come to the assistance of some other railways in such matters. The Grand Trunk pays ,a reasonable charge for the use of these engines.

I spoke a moment ago of the necessity of avoiding waste and duplication. We have made, I think, a reasonable and, certainly, a bona fide effort, to bring that about during the pas^ year. The report which I am about to read is lengthy; but I think it worth while- to read it so that hon. members and the. people generally may know that something substantial has been accomplished under .the direction of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) in avoiding waste and duplication during the past year. One report is dated the 26th day of March. I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals early in that- month to get for me a statement from the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence of what they had accomplished during the eight or nine months in which they had been in operation. From reports which had reached me I came to the conclusion that they had accomplished a good deal but I was equally of the opinion that not only the people of the country but the. members of this House were largely ignorant of what had been done. Mr. W. M. Neal, by whom this report has been prepared, is the secretary of this association. The association itself is composed of representatives of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway, the "Grand Trunk Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway, *the Government 'System of railways and the New York 'Central. It has organized its work under six heads. There is a; special committee on war and national defence, an administrative committee, a commission on car service, a committee on passenger transportation, a committee on tariffs and .statistics and a'committee on materials and supplies. The report is as follows:
In addition to the information embodied in our communication of the 21st inst., relative to the work of the Canadian Railway Association for National 'Defence, it will no doubt be of interest to you to learn of the details of the organization of the Association itself.
In accordance with arrangements which were made at preliminary meetings of representatives of the Dominion Government and the railways, an invitation was issued to railways operating in 'Canada to attend a conference at Montreal on October 23rd, 1917, for the purpose of formulating a Central Railway Organization and outlining its working policies. This conference was held on the date mentioned in the offices of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Windsor Street Station, Montreal, all of the principal and a number of the smaller lines being represented.
After. explaining what was desired in the way of co-ordinating the facilities and efforts of the various lines so as to permit of the efficient handling of the extremely 'heavy volume of traffic which it was expected the railways would be called upon to move during

the winter and conservation of fuel, motive power and man power, it was decided to appoint a Committee composed of the executives of some of the larger lines who would direct the policy of the new organization, which was to he known as "The Canadian Railway Association for National Defence."
A Special Committee on War and National Defence was formed, with the following per-, sonnel:-
