Very full and -complete information as to what has been accomplished is. contained in the report of March 21, 1918, to which I shall now give attention. It is addressed to the Minister of Railways and is as fob lows:
"" As requested in your letter of 18th inst., following is statement of the operations of the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence :-
Summary of work done by Canadian Railways working under the direction of the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence.
October 23rd, 1917, to March 20th, 1918.
I invite the attention of hon. gentlemen to what has been accomplished, because it strikes me that the result really does indicate that this association, and the methods which it has followed, have been of great

advantage to us during the past autumn and winter.
Fuel conservation.-Saving through reduced passenger services and heavy loading of cars and trains during ensuing year under practices now in vogue (estimated), -500,000 tons.
Increased movement of freight by diversions during congestions arising from unusually severe winter weather, 516,565 tons.
Increase in delivery of empty box cars from United States to Canada under arrangements made by association, 14,260.
Estimated increase -in car efficiency during current year through improved handling and heavier loading of cars equivalent to 300,000 car trips.
Freedom from serious- congestion in both eastern and western Canada such as was experienced ini the winter of 1916-1917 and in the United States during the winter now coming to a close.
Prompt filling of requirements of overseas transports at ports served by Canadian Railways.
Increase in coal deliveries to Canada from United States, 285,000 tons.
Increases in freight traffic by diversion of cars from over-burdened routes.
On orders issued by the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence and arrangements made with the railways interested, a total of fourteen thousand seven hundred and fifty-nine loaded cars have been diverted from congested routes to others which were comparatively free. These cars, many of which were loaded with grain and coal contained approximately five hundred and sixteen thousand five hundred and sixty-five tons of freight.
Included in the diversions wrere twenty-one hundred and eighty cars which were billed eastbound via the Canadian Pacific Railway through Fort William for points in Ontario and Quebec and diverted via the Soo Line from Emerson to Sault Ste. Marie, being returned to the Canadian Pacific Railway at the latter point, thus relieving the heavily taxed line east from Fort William.
Diversions of freight routed via' Canadian Pacific Railway from Fort William for Eastern Canada points and overseas were made to the Canadian Northern Railway at Port Arthur, the cars being returned to the Canadian Pacific Railway at Sudbury and Ottawa. These diversions via Port Arthur total up to date four hundred and throe oars and the arrangement calls for continued diversion as necessary up to forty cars per day.
On-e result of these two switches in the movement of eastbound freight is an increase in the movement of grain by rail from the head of the lakes of approximately three and one half million bushels, in addition to avoiding congestion at the terminals in that territory, and expediting the general movement of cars through that gateway.
The handling of traffic from the Niagara Frontier to Ontario points during the winter months, when the entire burden is thrown upon the railways operating between Buffalo and Toronto owing to the suspension of ferry service across Lake Erie, up to this year caused a great deal of delay to freight and cars and interfered with the requisite coal deliveries for consumption in Ontario to such an extent as to have been partly responsible for the fuel short-

age in that province during the winter of 19161917.
This year, at the first hint of trouble, the Administrative Committee of the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence, after going over the situation in detail, delegated one of their members, Mr. F. F. Backus, General Manager of the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway, as the representative of the Association to take full charge of operation of lines between the Frontier and Toronto, with authority to switch traffic and engines from one line to another as the conditions day by day might demand.
Under Mr. Backus' direction, cars were diverted from the overburdened Grand Trunk railway route to the joint line furnished by the M.C.R.R., T.H. & B., and Canadian Pacific railway, to the number of five thousand and eighty-one, which means that the total movement of freight from the United States to Canada via the Niagara gateway was increased to that extent. These diversions extended over the period from January 6th to March 6th when conditions became practically normal and the necessity for further transfer of cars from the routing prescribed on the billing disappeared.
About sixty per cent of the five thousand and eighty-one cars by which the movement from the Frontier was increased as described above contained coal so that the coal receipts in Ontario during the two months mentioned were increased by approximately one hundred and fifty thousand tons.
Arrangements were made with the United States railway authorities at Washington whereby empty box cars ordered to Canada to assist in making up the number of cars due us on the interchange with United States lines were diverted to the Delaware and Hudson railway where they are loaded with coal, principally for points in the province of Quebec, thus increasing the coal receipts in this province, as well as providing box cars for the movement of exports to the United States. Under this arrangement five thousand eight hundred empty box oars were turned over to the Delaware and Hudson railway, and up to date three thousand eight hundred and thirty-five have been loaded with coal as above, containing approximately one hundred and thirty-five thousand tons of coal. It is the intention to continue this arrangement as long as empty cars are being sent to Canada as at present.
During the past few weeks the movement of shipments from points in Ontario to Quebec and the Maritime Provinces has been increased by the diversion of 1,641 carloads from the Canadian Pacific railway and Grand Trunk railway to the Canadian Northern railway at Toronto, in order to relieve the lines of the former between Toronto and Montreal and hasten recovery from conditions arising from the series of severe storms from which the railways suffered in Ontario during January and early February.
Another object sought by the Association was the avoidance of a repetition of the shortage of foodstuffs which existed in the Maritime Provinces during the winter of 1916-1917 owing to the heavy movement of overseas supplies which had to be given preference over the lines east of Montreal and tended at times to crowd out domestic shipments. With this end in view cars were transferred from the heavily burdened Canadian Pacific railway route from Montreal to St. John to the Canadian Government railways at Quebec and Ste. Rosalie, the movement
of freight to the Maritime Provinces being increased in this way by 1,565 carloads or approximately 45,000 tons of freight.
Diversions of cars from one line to another similar to those given in detail above were made a't Sudbury, Ottawa, North Bay, Winnipeg and Saskatoon.
Handling of Grain, Flour and Coal, Western Canada.
In Western Canada the activities of the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence, or the "Railways War Board" as it has come to be popularly known amongst the shipping public, were directed chiefly to keeping up the deliveries of grain andi flour to the East, both for domestic consumption and shipment overseas and maintaining the requisite movement of cars from the mines in Alberta. It is admitted that, in the face of a winter of operating conditions of almost unprecedented severity, when engines froze up on the road, water supplies disappeared overnight and at times the men remained on duty only at greatest hardship, the demands of the transports and Eastern millers were met and coal was delivered to the prairie cities and towns with a regularity and promptness that could hardly have been expected by the uninitiated had they been able to foresee the obstacles which had to be overcome. Preparations which are being made in the west now for improvements during the coming summer it is anticipated will permit of .a still better service being provided next winter.
The views of the western public on the accomplishments of the railways in Western Canada, are, perhaps, voiced in the following extract from an editorial appearing in the Moosejaw Evening Times of March 11th, in referring to one of the bulletins issued by the Railways War Board:
This winter we (The Canadian Railway Association) are determined to keep Canada's traffic rolling smoothly and with speed even though last year's conditions repeat themselves, (extract from bulletin).
Well, last year's conditions did repeat themselves with a vengeance and Canada's traffic has been handled more smoothly and efficiently in spite of even a greater scarcity of labour.
The arrangements made by the Western Committee of the Association included the distribution of grain and coal cars between lines as they were required regardless of ownership and the same action was taken in the case of water cars when water supplies failed on account of the severe weather and water for locomotives had to be hauled long distances.
Car Supply.
When the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence was formed on October 23rd, 1917, one of the first tasks with which it was confronted was the recovery from the United States railways of some 20,679 Canadian owned freight cars located in the United States in excess of the number of cars of United States ownership in this country, that is, the Canadian lines had less than ninety per cent of the number of cars owned by them and required to handle traffic currently. The railways individually had been pressing their American connections to return their cars but had been unable to make satisfactory progress.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, in his exposition of the railway situation of the country as it is at the present time, went back to the initiation of the policy of the Transcontinental railway in the year 1903. To be exact he should have gone much further, because the situation that we have to face to-day is very serious, not on account of the policy which was adopted in 1903 for the creation of a. second transcontinental railway, nor the policy that was adopted of having a third transcontinental railway, but, as the right hon. gentleman .from his very remarks showed, the situation is serious on account of one o.f 'the oldest-in fact, the oldest railway-that we have, the Grand Trunk railway itself. The Prime Minister, in his re. view of the situation, should have gone as far back as the year 1850, when the Grand Trunk railway was introduced in Canada. At that time railway construction in the world was still comparatively new, in fact,

to say that settlement is going in these very rapidly; indications are 'that the traffic in that district will become more and more extensive.
The Transcontinental railway has not been as great a success as it might have been, and one of the reasons why the traffic on that road has not expanded more rapidly 'than it has is found in the death of Mr. Hays, the late general manager of the Grand Trunk railway, to whom is due the credit of the initiation of the enterprise. He was a man of great energy, resource and ability, and had he lived the railway would he more prosperous than it is at present. Indeed, his death was a national calamity.
The construction of the Canadian Northern^ railway was not entered upon as a national enterprise; it grew from a local undertaking until it matured into a transcontinental system. The Prime Minister said a moment ago that that railway had as great a future as any railway in Canada.
I say that it has as great a future as any railway on the continent of America. That may be a broad assertion, but it is to be remembered that there is no better land on the whole continent than that between the cities of Edmonton, and Winnipeg; every foot of the Canadian Northern line between those cities is revenue-producing. From Winnipeg to the head, of the lakes, the rai'-way, after leaving the city of Winnipeg, passes through a marshy land which may not be productive now, but which will be productive later on. Then it enters the valley of the Rainy river, one of the best sections of country on the continent. Leaving the head of lake Superior the line does not follow the lake, because of the district being barren and rocky, hut enters the clay belt, which will probably he productive. From Sudibury to Ottawa, from Ottawa to Montreal and. from Montreal to Quebec the line passes through a good country. Undoubtedly, therefore, the Canadian Northern railway system has* a great future. I am not disposed to criticise the promoters of this enterprise, Mackenzie and Mann. They displayed great energy and great enterprise, and I firmly believe that but for the war they would have brought the road to satisfactory completion. When the Government proposed to acquire the road I did not object, because I thought that the property was a good one; the only question was as to the terms under which it should be acquired. That is the view which I take of the whole situation..

The Government now proposes to launch into a new enterprise, that of acquiring the Grand Trunk railway itself. The history of the Grand Trunk Tailway is not a satisfactory one. The Grand Trunk has been in existence about sixty years. It passes through one of the best parts of the American continent, undoubtedly through the Ibest part of Ontario; it ought to he and it is productive. If it is not as profitable or prosperous an enterprise as it should have been, that is due to. two things. First, the management has always been in London, England. In my judgment, no greater mistake could have been made. It is inconceivable that the management of -a great railway system, covering almost the whole of this continent, could be satisfactorily carried on from the city of London. Second, the system has been overloaded with bad securities. That the Grand Trunk railway system can be made a profitable enterprise I have no doubt. I do not pretend to be an expert in these matters, but, applying the ordinary principles of common sense; looking on the advantages enjoyed by this railway, its splendid location, its line from the great centre of Chicago to the fine harbour of Portland, I think that the Grand Trunk railway system should be productive of good results and profitable returns. For the present I do not condemn the idea of taking this railway over; everything depends on the terms. But I warn the members of the Government that if they acquire that property they will find it loaded with absolutely unproductive and utterly worthless securities. In this condition may be found the great danger of such negotiations as my Tight hon. friend has suggested. But since the .Government contemplate taking this step, I shall not condemn it at this time. The idea is one which deserves consideration, and I, therefore, would not go further than that.	'
The only thing as to which I am disappointed in the statement made by my right hon. friend is that the has been very vague in regard to the organization under which he is going to place the present Canadian Northern railway. We heard yesterday that the Government, before re-organizing the Canadian. Northern railway, were waiting for the receipt of the report of the arbitrators as to the price to- be paid for the stock of that enterprise. Why wait for that? What more information than the Government has to-day will it have when it receives the award of the arbitrators? To-

day, under the terms of the Act which was passed last year, the Government is the absolute owner of the Canadian Northern railway. We purchased the stock. The purchase price was not paid because the amount had not been fixed. The question as to the amount of the purchase price was referred to arbitration by the two parties, to the contract. But the contract was made by the two parties, and, therefore, to-day we are the absolute owners of the Canadian Northern, and the question whether the amount that we have to pay for the stock be large or small, is of no concern whatever. Aa the owners of the Canadian Northern railway, if we are to make full use of it, we ought immediately to re-organize and operate it. I cannot see that it is good or sound policy to wait until we know how wre stand as to the price we have to pay. We should go on with the reorganization at once. The Prime Minister, in speaking of the re-organization, [DOT]spoke upon a subject which everybody has in mind, that is to say, that we should keep that enterprise free from political patronage. Political patronage has been the bane of railway administration in Canada.
1 do not blame one party more than the other , for that. The former Liberal Government did their best to eliminate political patronage, and while I do not say that we succeeded completely in eliminating it, we made a good deal of reform. If political patronage is to be eliminated from railway administration in Canada-and my right lion, friend has particularly insisted upon that point,-the plan which he has suggested does not seem to be conducive of that result. If you have any board of directors whicb is appointed by the Government, you will not eliminate political patronage.
May I -make a suggestion to my right hon. friend, and to the other members of the Government, as to a method of eliminating patronage? The city of Washington, district of Columbia, is federal property; it is not a state. It does not form part of the Union; it is independent territory. It is, I understand, extremely well administered. I have never heard of graft of any kind, nor have I heard of political patronage, in the administration of the city of Washington. In years past I frequently had to visit that city, and my right hon. friend has in recent years had to go there very often, but I have not heard, and I do not think he has ever heard anything but commendation of the
administration of the city of Washington, D.C. How is it administered? It is administered by a commission composed of three commissioners, one appointed by the party in office, the second by the party in opposition, and the third is an officer of the army. The Uunited States army_ was never a very numerous body, hut it is well known that its staff of officers is a very highly cultured and fine body of men with a high sense of honour and absolutely honest. I do not know by whom the third commissioner, an officer of the army, is appointed. I think he is appointed by the President. Be this as it may, this is a body which is absolutely non-political. As to the elimination of patronage from railway administration in Canada, if patronage is to be eliminated-and every hon. member in this House either wants or, because the opinion of the people behind him is so strong, at least pretends that he wants to eliminate patronage,-I do not know of any system which would come nearer to the elimination of patronage than such a system which I have just suggested.

We were discussing the relative value of debenture stock when the House rose at six o'clock. I have here a statement of the annual meeting of the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in which the president, Lord Shaughnessy, says:
In order to avoid this undesirable situation the Company decided, with the consent of Parliament, to utilize consolidated debenture stock for the purchase or conversion of existing bonds, and to provide funds for building or acquiring such additional mileage as might appear to be required from time to time for the advantage of the country and the company. ' This consolidated debenture stock is perpetual and irredeemable, differing from a mortgage bond in that it gives no right of foreclosure in the event of default. The holders have a first claim on the revenues of the company for their semi-annual dividends after the working expenses and taxes or fines have been paid, and the contract demands of existing bondholders have been satisfied. If by any chance the company failed to pay, within a fixed period, the dividend accrued on the consolidated debenture stock the holders of that stock would become the Shareholders of the company and would control its affairs until the default was made good, when the property would automatically pass back to the preference and ordinary shareholders.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it may be in this case that there is an agreement between the makers of this debenture stock and the holders on some special basis, or some special arrangement may have been made, but there is no question but that the debenture stock is a liability of the company, and such being the case the total liabilities of'the Canadian Northern Railway Company would stand at $438,000,000. The Prime Minister this- afternoon, if I heard him aright, made the statement that the road was valued by the Dray-ton-Acworth Commission at $497,000,000. I have here the report of that commission and it is strange that we can find so many conflicting figures in the same report. The Prime Minister explained this afternoon that he is not familiar with figures, and had a statement prepared which is practically the same as the one I gave to the House yesterday as to the liabilities of thS Canadian Northern Railway Company, hut he did not quite agree with me as to the cost of the road. It has magnificent hotels, excellent terminal facilities, ample yard room at [Quebdc, Ottawa, (Montreal and other cities; there is no- comparison between this, railway and the others in the matter of terminals, road/beds or rails. I do not believe members of this committee wish to go back into the political history of the railroad situation in 'this country. We have a situation here to face. The previous Parliament assum'ed obligations of $437,000,000, and there is a farce being carried on in Toronto- to-day, -called an arbitration board, to arrive at the value of a worthless stock, a stock that is not only worthless, but which carries with it a liability o-f something like $147,000,000 of unguaranteed securities. That furnishes no information, whatever to this *Committee. We paid out of one pocket into the other. But we want to know' where this money finally landed, who got it, who are the people holding the unguaranteed securities; what relation do they stand in to- the promoters of this road, to the Mackenzie and Mann people. It is not furnishing information to the Committee to say that we paid to the -Canadian Northern $25,000,000, and paid it out in amounts of $2,000,000,	$12,000,000 or $15,000,000.
That is simply pl-aying the same old game. The Canadian Northern paid to Mackenzie and Mann, and Mackenzie and Mann to the Northern Construction, Company, and the Northern Construction- Company back to Mackenzie and Mann.	We do not
want that -condition to continue. If we have -assumed, the liabilities of . the Canadian Northern Railway system, let us put the cards- on- the table, take our loss, and proceed to have this railroad organized in a business way, so that we can run the road to the best possible advantage to the country and to the railroad itself. Mackenzie and Mann can-. not possibly have any interest in the propel operation of this road; they have no interest whatever in making dividends on this road now. 1 cannot- conceive how the 
Government are taking away from a certain syndicate a railroad system, and at the same time leaving the same people in charge of its management. We are told we have acquired the stock and the ownership. The question of the -details of settlement of what we are to' pay, not exceeding $10,000,000 for 600,000 -shares of stock, lias nothing whatever to do with the management of the road. If the Government are sincere in the matter, the first thing they should consider is the management. The question of arbitration has nothing whatever to do with Mackenzie and Mann. As soon as the decision to take it over was arrived at, there should have been put in control of the road independent people, who wo-uld take it and develop it for the benefit of the country. I do not know what the directors of this road get, but I can easily understand that the Mackenzie and Mann ring would be willing to pay not less than $1,000,000 a year to be left in charge of it, for the side issues, the subsidiary companies. Where do they buy coal? Who is doing the construction? We were told there was $11,000,000 expended last year in extensions. There was no mention made of that until to-day.
We were told Iby the Minister of Railways that there were no extensions and no new undertakings. The cost of the road to the country has increased from $13,000,000 to $15,000,000 within the last year. It would have been 'better if iwe had paid the Mackenzie and Mann outfit $10,000,000 last year and got rid of them and put some person, in charge of the road to manage it as a going concern. If the Prime Minister thinks that the people -are willing to maintain Mackenzie and -Mann in control of that road he is very much mistaken. There is great value in the road; it runs through good territory and can he made a paying concern, hut if we leave it in charge of men who exploit it for their own personal gain the country will have to stand the loiss. I cannot understand why we should wait for an arbitration board to determine whether we are to pay $9,000,000 or $10,000,000 for this road, and still leave the same people in charge of it. Before any -member of this committee would make an investment in any undertaking he would want to know who the management were and what their policy was. In, this case we are paying out money and taking no interest whatever in the management of the undertaking. As a matter of fact, I do not know what we are voting this money for; no explanation has been given. The first item is for a payment to the Dominion

Government, and there is another item for payment of debenture stock. I always understood that debenture stock was not redeemable; that it was perpetual. If there is an understanding iwith the owners of the stock that $12,000,000 of it is to be redeemed this year we should know who these owners are, what their relation is to the Mackenzie and Mann outfit, and on what terms this money is being paid. I do not believe that a cent has ever been paid for this debenture stock; most likely it has been given as a bonus to some bondholders, who should be willing to wait for the interest on their investment. Let us work this proposal out to the best possible advantage on behalf of the people. Let us quit trying to fool ourselves o.r any person else with regard to our obligation in the matter. It is useless for us to say that this is not a direct obligation; of course, it is an obligation on the country, which will add just so much to our debt. We should have a full detailed report with regard to the company and its liabilities and with regard to the subsidiary companies and their liabilities, so that we shall know what we are doing.
Mr. 1H. A. MACKIE:	il believe that I
voice the feelings of the men from the West when I say that we received with a great deal of satisfaction the declaration of the Prime Minister this evening. We regret, however, that he was not more pronounced in certain respects. We should have been better pleased had he stated outright that it was the policy of the Government to adopt the principle of public ownership, not only of railways but of all other great means of transportation. We regret that we must wait until a time which is not defined for the Government to take control and operation of the road in question. I do not doubt that these matters have received serious consideration and that the ministers must be worried about them, but the people are also worried; they are wondering what the end of it all will be. Instead of waiting for any commission to declare that the stock of these gentlemen is worth $10,000,000 or less, I would declare that they are entitled to a ten-year penitentiary sentence. I do not know why they should be retained in the service of the country for any great length of time, unless it be for the benefit of succeeding ages; that is, to allow these gentlemen sufficient time for their financial morality to become so corrupt that it will cease to be contagious. We have heard
a number of statements about the calamitous circumstances which have brought about the present railway situation, but nothing has been said in a definite way as to why we should adopt the principle of the public ownership of railways and of the great means of transportation in Canada. We find the railway situation to he deplorable, indeed, and we propose that the Government shall do certain things, not because any principle has. been enunciated because a set of circumstances makes it impossible to do otherwise. I wish to deal this evening with the principle of public ownership. I shall endeavour to show that it is the right principle to adopt for western conditions, and I will defy contradiction so far as the principle is concerned.
I shall, at the same time, endeavour to show that this is the method which ought to be adopted in order to bring 'the East and the West closer together.
First, it is necessary thoroughly to understand the reason there is for the adoption of the public ownership of railways. We are convinced, having regard to the whole economic condition of Canada and the enormous freight and passenger rates which prevail, that the proportion of wealth which passes into the hands of private corporations is altogether too great. That fundamentally underlies the adoption of the principle of public ownership of railways, and it is our duty to examine that principle and see whether it will accomplish 'the object in view.
It is evident that there are two ways of reducing the cost of living, especially to the western people. These two methods differ essentially. The first I call patriotic, and the second I call unpatriotic. The one which I have designated as unpatriotic is the one which was advocated by the Opposition when they were in power, but which they did not dare to carry out during their whole period of administration. I refer to the abolition of protective tariff, upon which the industries of the East exist, and without which they cannot exist. A protective tariff which operates'to the advantage of the eastern manufacturers operates equally to the disadvantage of the western farmers. But there is a compensating advantage to the western farmer. It creates for him a national, a Canadian, market, for his western produce. The removal of the protective tariff system which has been so successful in building up the eastern provinces, would be a betrayal of the confidence of those who have invested their capital in protected industries. What-

ever modification may in the future take place in the tariff, it must be based upon the consideration of existing industries and be fair to the interests of both the producer and the consumer. That, however, would be one method of reducing the cost of living to the western farmer; of increasing the reward paid to the man on the plains who forms the basis and foundation of the growth and progress of the West. That is the method which I have designated as unpatriotic, because it involves the placing of East and West in opposition, and creating economic factors of the people east and west of the Jakes.
The other method of decreasing the cost of living is by cheapening transportation facilities, and it is here that I believe the declaration of the Premier lacks strength. He told us there would be public ownership of certain railways how. He indicated that, at a time not far distant, the Grand Trunk Pacific would become part of the Government Railway system. He also stated that the Grand Trunk would also, at some future time, become part of that system, and he gave us the idea that in the very distant future the Canadian Pacific must also necessarily be one of the railways included in that system of public ownership. The principle of public ownership is the cheapening rates in transportation, both passenger and freight, and I cannot see how, unless we declare for public ownership of all means of transportation in this country, we shall arrive at the object of public ownership of railways. The second method, therefore, of reducing the cost of living, and particularly to the western man, is Government ownership, and Government ownership of the great vehicles of transportation is one Which has for its end a more patriotic and beneficial object than the abolition of the tariff. I want to deal with the principles underlying Government ownership and operation of railways, and to show how a Government is far better situated than a private corporation to supply the transportation needs of a people. Those who have evinced disbelief in public ownership usually speak as though the present operation and control of railways were the most perfect conceivable, and they imply that the utter corruptness and dishonesty of politicians make' the control of a vast number of men and the working of a great department out of the question. All such arguments are against the dishonesty of our politicians and not against the principle of public ownership of railways. Let us first consider this issue. Are our poli-
ticians at Ottawa more corrupt and dishonest than the heads of our great corporations? I deny utterly that they are, and this afternoon the Prime Minister stated that, in order that political patronage might be removed, an independent board would be constituted, and he emphasized the fact that it would be absolutely separate and that there would be no interference with it whatever. I deny that our politicians at Ottawa are more corrupt than the heads of private corporations. We apply to our men in public life tests far more searching than those which we apply to our great so-called captains of industry. If we turned upon the heads of corporations the same light that we turn upon politicians, the result would be something astounding. To digress, I may say that all I have to do is to point to what has happened in the United States in recent months, or in the last year and a half, and you have the answer there- private corporations and scandals. As for the patrons of industries who are supposed to be so honest, their contribution to the advancement of this country has mainly consisted in gazing sleepily through the windows of a private car at the laying out of stations and town-sites by the actual railroad pioneers, and in abstracting profits which rightfully belonged to the people of Canada. In addition to this consideration of their usefulness, there has been a tremendous amount of land subsidies and money subsidies, .and other assistance of one sort or another, and that is what has brought about the condition which exists to-day and which compelled the Premier to make the declaration which he did this afternoon. Consequently the proposition before us is this-had we not better build and operate our own lines of transportation than furnish the financial strength and backing to others to do it, and permit them to rob us unduly and deny us any say as to what the rates Shall be?	*
No one really believes that the operation of railways by .private corporations is a perfect policy. Between cheap freight and passenger rates and large dividends there is a wide divergence, and the creation of a railway commission is sufficient proof that the Government i.s aware that private corporations cannot serve their own interest and that of the people at one and the same time. The creation of the Railway Commission was a virtual declaration in favour of state control of railways.
I wish to give .the- House a few facts as to why we should stop .pursuing the policy

which has b-een adopted by both parties in Canada, and why it is time that we should now adopt a policy of public ownership of railways. Up to June, 1916, assuming that the money represented by bonds and consolidated debenture stock was actually invested in railways in Canada, the total would be $1,045,608,331. This information is to be found at page Xll of the Blue Book for 1916. The figures for 1917 have been prepared, but not printed, and the information which I received from Mr. J. L. Payne, the comptroller, was that the figures for 1917 would not Ibe materially altered, except to increase the bonded indebtedness of railways by about $50,000,000, which is a mere trifle in these days. The amount of common stock outstanding in 1916 was $848,269,448. This information is also to be found at page Xll of the Blue Book of 1916. The total is $1,893,877,819. This is without taking into consideration the $50,000,000 of which I spoke a moment ago. In addition to these sums, the Dominion Government, provincial governments, municipalities and other sources have given cash aid as follows *

These figures do not take into consideration the purchase of the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds, aggregating $33,116,000, by the Government, nor do they take into consideration that the Dominion has constructed and now operates the eastern division of the Transcontinental railway, upon which, up to March 31, 1916, there had been an expenditure of $156,701,210. It would be interesting to know the difference between these billiohs of capital and the actual cost of the roads, with a fair profit for promotion and construction. Hearsay evidence establishes that about twenty-five per cent goes to promotion; that is to say, that Canadians are paying, in the shape of freight and passenger rates, interest on a tfemendous amount of money which never went into the actual building of railways.
It has been the claim of the Liberal party that competition in transportation facilities is the cure for all evils of rates which appear to be too exorbitant. To this I desire to take exception. Competition only aggravates the existing evils of western transportation. Let me explain. Canada possesses more mileage in proportion to its population than any ether country in the world..
One mile of steel exists , to every twenty-seven inhabitants of this land,, and when we consider that this includes the more densely peopled provinces of the East one naturally wonders what the country consisting of the four provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia possesses in the way of miles of steel per head of the population. The figures of these provinces is given in this volume of statistics, pages 25 and 26, as follows:-

Despite these astounding figures, however, the West has less railway mileage to its area than any other part of the country. And'it is right here that the waste of competition is apparent. Great tracks of country lie untapped by railway service while our uneconomic friends, the Liberal party, preach the policy of constructing duplicate tracks paralleling one another for miles. Where the entire country might be served by one line, wre have three, and a difficulty with regard to reasonable freight rates is created by the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific which will not be overcome for generations. The fault of railway companies in this country has not been alone that they overcharged for their service, it is a fault far more subtle than that, it is the fault that railroads are not constructed [DOT]with a view to supplying the country's needs, but are largely constructed on guaranteed loans or money subsidies with an insane idea as to competition.
Let us consider further this question of competition. Mill, the great English economist in his famous and monumental work Principles of Political Economy, in what is considered the best chapters of that work, The Cost of Production, lays down the proposition that there is a limit, sternly and rigidly defined by economic law, to the extent to which competition can cheapen the commodity. That limit, he declares, is the cost to produce the commodity, paying a living wage to the labourers involved, a rate of interest to the capital invested equal to what the average of the money market will afford, and the cost of the maintenance of the capital involved. Below that economic line it is impossible to go, for should it be exceeded, capital is at once withdrawn from the production of the commodity, and the condition rights itself by the scarcity of the commodity due to that withdrawal.
Now this applies to the transportation cost in the West. The price of freight



Prime Minister has taken a most important step towards absolute public ownership, and I trust it will be a shorter time than he has given us reason to believe before some plan is worked out to take over all the railways in Canada, so that we in the West may be able to live in closer union with the people of the East as a result of cheaper freight and passenger rates.

However, the Act provides that the Government may pay to the minority shareholders the same proportion which, under the arbitration, they will be held to pay to the majority shareholders. There are outstanding shares of the Canadian Northern Quebec, the Quebec and Lake St. John, and the Duluth, Winnipeg and Western railways that we did not acquire. The minority shares that the horn gentleman refers to are minority shares in the Canadian Northern enterprises which are held overseas, and these minority shares can be acquired under the terms of the statute of last session. subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Only the importance of the transportation question ^ould induce me at this late stage of the session to project my.^lf into the present discussion. On the Budget debate I spoke at considerable length with reference to that question, and I crave the indulgence of the House to-night while I present a few figures, and refer in a brief manner historically to the subject of transportation.
I am sure it must have been gratifying not only to the members of the House, but *to the country at large to have the right hon. leader of the House (Sir Robert Borden) make the very important statement which' he made this afternoon. I could not help but think that after all it may have *been due to the pressure that has been exercised-at least to some extent-and undoubtedly to the uneasiness of the House generally with reference to this great question, as well as to the feeling that exists *throughout the country as to the necessity of solving this problem, that the Prime Minister made this speech. Personally, I was extremely gratified, because Canada, in spite of herself, is face to face with the necessity of administering a large system of /railroads under public ownership. As I remarked in the House the other day, I thought the courteous and able Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) probably slipped a linguistic cog when he said that Parliament last session as well as the *country seemed anxious to take hold of the Canadian Northern, I was under the impression. and still am of the opinion, that that Statement on the hon. gentleman's part does not represent the real condition of affairs. .I do not think the House and the country have been anxious to take over the

Canadian Northern, -or to take over any system of railways, in. view of the conditions under which that taking over has to be done. The Prime Minister told ns this afternoon that had! Parliament not come to the rescue the road -would have been forced into liquidation, and he expatiated on the injury that would have resulted to the public credit if this road had been allowed to go into liquidation and into the hands of a receiver. The Prime Minister's speech must have inspired the House with confidence -in his earnestness and good intentions. But I say, with all due deference to him. and to the late Parliament-if Parliament was responsible, but I prefer to put the blame on the shoulders of the late and old governments; I do not think the policy pursued with regard to the Canadian Northern, was the right policy to adopt in the case of that railroad or of any other in a similar situation-it is not because of the action of Parliament or of the country that these roads find themselves in difficulties. The Canadian Northern for the last twenty or twenty-five years, have been applying to this Parliament and to the Provincial Legislatures .for aid to build mileage, and the reason they usually urge for that was that the people were clamouring for this accommodation. In my judgment, whenever a squeak was uttered by a settler for assistance, or for railway accommodation, the (big noise and the real' pressure came from the proprietors of this railroad. They were the ones that were anxious to build these lines of railway; they were the ones that besieged and badgered the federal and provincial Governments. They have been knocking at the doors of the Provincial Legislatures and of the Dominion Parliament for almost two decades and a half, and, in my judgment, the responsibility for the present situation rests with them.
If as the result of their manipulations, or of their failure to make a success of the road, they find themselves in great difficulties, find that they .are unable to meet their obligations, on whom should the blame rest? Not upon this Parliament, not upon the provincial parliaments, not upon the people of Canada, but upon the railroad manipulators themselves. Then should they not have been obliged to take the consequences of their own folly? As a publicist, I have grown pretty tired of that old cry: "We must guard the credit of Canada." When the Byron Walkers and the other great "financiers," and the exploiters get into trouble they hold up their hands

in alarm and say: "Lest the credit of Canada shall suffer, in Heaven's name, come to our rescue." And we, the people of Canada have been coming to their rescue for the last thirty or forty years. I am sure that as the House listened this afternoon to the words of the Prime Minister when he told of the campaign of raids that had been made on the public treasury by these exploiters, we must have almost blushed when we recalled that year after year these exploiters came and raided, and raided, and raided the public treasury. Are WE, therefore, to blame if, as a result of their own folly, they find that they have reached the end of their financial tether? Eather in my judgment would it be better, and I believe it to he the judgment of all thoughtful Canadians who have studied this question, that an example should be made of them, and that they should be obliged to take the consequences of their own folly. Why should this Parliament and this country be obliged to come to the rescue on every possible occasion to bolster up, say, the Bank of Commerce, and to help this or the other corporation to escape from the results of their own improvidence and folly? No. I say that this Parliament and this Government should stand .solid and say: "Gentlemen, you have committed this folly yourselves, you .alone are responsible, therefore you must take the consequences." Canada can take care of its own credit. Canada is a great nation, with marvellous resources, and we can afford to let one of these corporations go into liquidation, take the consequences of its folly, and by so doing we will put ian end to a repetition and to all that kind of thing. We were under no responsibility, moral or legal, to take over the Canadian Northern Railway under the conditions that we have acquired it. Members of this Parliament-and we have not been very long in session-will recall debate after debate on the question as to the liabilities of the Canadian Northern railway. One day we are told that the liabilities-and it is ispoken under your breath-are $300,000,000. A few days later we are told that the liabilities of this corporation have risen to $350,000,000, and, tell it not in Gath, we were supposed to stand aghast when we were informed still later that they were $400,000,000. And now, does the Prime Minister tell us from his seat in this House this afternoon that the liabilities are $300,000,000,	$350,000,000,	$400,-
000,000? No, they have risen in one jump to the astounding figure of $438,000,000. The right hon. leader of the House tells

us that we are to get this system of railroads at a price that will not be more than $44,000 per mile on the ten thousand miles which constitute the system. I can tell the Prime Minister that the system which the people of Manitoba constructed some twenty years ago, and which some years ago was acquired by the Canadian Northern, cost only $9,000 per mile to construct. Y'et we are asked to rejoice over the great bargain that we are going to make in acquiring this system at a capitalization not greater than $44,000 per mile. The Prime Minister gave us figures to indicate that, while the liability was $433,264,377.67, the assets we would receive would amount to $528,427,000. Now, where that argument does not hold water in my judgment is here: If we take over the Canadian Northern system-and we have to take it over- the baby, as I said the other day, has been put on our lap to nurse; we were not the authors of the baby; we did not bring it into existence, yet it is going to sit squalling on our lap for the rest of time, and we must take care of it for all time to come. If we take over this system, as we must, what is the situation? Owing to the folly, the criminal folly of the exploiters who have manipulated railroads in this country for the last twenty-five or thirty years, we find that we have to take over this and other systems with an approximate mileage probably anywhere from a thousand to three thousand miles, which will not be of any practical use to the country at the present time, and which may not be of any practical use for a long time to come, if ever. Take the road built through the Mountains by the Canadian Northern. I suppose some hon. members are here who went over that railroad on that celebrated excursion two years ago. They must have been convinced of the folly it was to build through the Yellowhead Pass a railroad to parallel the Grand Trunk Pacific; at this stage of the country's development. And then to go down to Kamloops, down the valley of the Thompson river and parallel the Canadian Pacific system to the coast. In my judgment some of those duplications will not for a long time, earn enough to pay for the stationery to set down the quantity of axle grease that, will be required on them. Then you have the other railroads built around the north shore of Lake Superior, which, of course, are for the present entirely superfluous, and in the case of the Canadian Northern railway, will not be a productive portion of the road, for, perhaps, years to come. Years ago. when my right hon.
friend the leader of the Opposition was in office and proposed the construction of the Transcontinental railway, I was very strongly opposed to that, and took a constituency and opposed his then Minister of the Interior,	Hon.-now Sir,-Clifford
Sifton, because I felt that that road was entirely premature,-and I hope to come back to that point later on. I then believed in the policy of imy right hon. friend the leader of the present Government (Sir Robert Borden). He then announced, and took that position before the country, that what was required was not another road around Lake Superior or another road through the mountains, but that we should double-track the Canadian Pacific railway, take it over and establish it as a railroad highway, giving all railroads running rights over that portion of the road. You see the prudence of a proposition of that kind is that it would have eliminated the vast expenditure necessary to construct this Transcontinental railway, and while on this point let me call the attention of the House to the fact that the Transcontinental railway which we were assured by the Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) would only cost the country $13,000,000, has already cost $200,000,000. And while the people had nothing whatever to do with bringing this child into existence, we also were obliged to have it dumped upon our lap, and there it will squall for many decades. So that we have these systems unloaded upon the country, regardless of our desires and of our necessities. That is where the tragedy .of our transportation problem comes in. It would be idle for me to enlarge upon this matter, although perhaps I may a little later on in my remarks refer to the responsibilities of different parties in the country for the unenviable position in which we find ourselves. I listened to a member of the Opposition the other day rail at this Government and at the former Government for the vast mistakes that had been made with regard to our transportation system. I could not help thinking that if hon. gentlemen opposite who took that view would look up the records of the Federal Parliament and of the provincial legislatures, they would find that in the matter of the responsibility for pouring money into the lap of these railroad exploiters and for establishing the present deplorable condition " honours ' have been carried off by the other side. I am not specially referring to this present " other side " because there is not a very important "other side" here; most of the

Liberal party, as I said in a former speech, are indentified with this side. But it is not worth w'hile indulging in recriminations against any particular set of politicians, because	politicians-or " statesmen " if you will-on both sides have been equally responsible for the, pouring of subsidies and subventions into the maw of exploiting corporations.
d should like to refer to one or two points made by the Prime Minister and by the leader of the Opposition. I will not say that the Prime Minister actually defended the arbitration proceedings now going on in Toronto, but he referred to them in a manner that led the House to conclude that he approved of them. At least he shares responsibility with the other side for the Act of the last Parliament under which the reference was made. I referred in a former speech to that arbitration. It did seem to me the height of folly. I could not conceive how public men, representatives of the people, with anything like a knowledge of the circumstances which have surrounded the building up of our transportation system, could agree-for I am sure the country does not agree-to a reference to arbitration of the question as to what amount should be paid to the Canadian Northern people for the crime that they, wittingly or unwittingly, have perpetrated against this country. They have unloaded upon us a system with a liability of $438,000,000-and that is far more than the system cost. They have the audacity-
I do not know whether, Mr. Chairman, by consulting the dictionary you could give me a stronger word; if so, I should like to. use it- to propose that the people of Canada shall contribute to them $10,000,000 as a reward for the outrage which they have perpetrated against the people. Perhaps I hold unusually strong views on this question, but I certainly hold that view, emphatically and unchangeably. If the decision is that they get $10,000,000 for the crime that they have perpetrated against the people, that amount will 'be added to the $438,000,000, making it $448,000,000; and we have only the financial figures, of the Canadian Northern Railway up to last September; if you add interest and everything that may have developed since, God knows where we will be as to the actual liability when we meet in the next session of Par'iament.
I said the other day that we were face to face with an appalling mess; but there it is; we have to face it. We have no option whatever in the matter. The balbs is on our lap and we must nurse it. We must 
proceed in the most businesslike way in order to solve this difficulty. Here is the only way in which we can make any progress and success. We have the Canadian Northern system. We must take the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk. The leader of the Opposition warned us this afternoon that the old Grand Trunk was so loaded, with obligations that we had better be very careful what we do with it. But the Grand Trunk is sponsor for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we must take that child, because the Grand Trunk Railway cannot itself hold the babe much longer. I suggest that we make this experiment: never mind the credit of Canada and the financiers of Canada-the dozen or so alleged financial big-wigs who live in Toronto and Montreal; let them attend to their own business for a while and let the people who perpetrated this folly on the public take the consequence of their own actions. Let the Grand Trunk Pacific go into liquidation, and if the Grand Trunk cannot hold the babe let us take mighty good care that the Grand Trunk does not unload it on us at anything like the expense with which the Canadian Northern has been unloaded on us or with anything like the consequences. I reiterate this point about the credit of Canada. Personally, I have grown tired' of hearing that oft-reiterated cry, and I think the people who do the paying-not who receive the dividends, mind you-are pretty well tired of it also. We want to settle this thing once and for all, We cannot borrow very much money in the markets of the Old Country now, anyway, because the war is on. We can do only what we are permitted to do by the British Government, and, perhaps, by the United States Government; so we need noi fear anything about the credit of Canada suffering. Let the credit of Canada slide just for once, and let us have one showdown. Is it always to be a case of heads the exporters win and tails the people lose?
I do not know whether the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) is perfectly satisfied. He asked me the other day to use my best endeavours to get the Government to adopt the recommendation of the Dray-ton-Acworth Commission that our national system of railways 'be operated by a commission independent of the Government, free from political interference and responsible only to Parliament, in order that patronage and political control or interference might be absolutely

eliminated. I said that I would use my best endeavour in the matter, and I have done so. I am not saying that because of anything I may have done to induce the Prime Minister to make the reasonably satisfactory announcement which he did this afternoon regarding the mode of management that shall be adopted. He came pretty nearly meeting my view. I hope he came as near to meeting the view of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). He did not say that the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth report' with regard to management would be adopted to the letter, but he came pretty close to it. He promised in unqualified terms that the [DOT] Government would provide for a management and administration of that system that would be entirely free from political control or manipulation. I believe the Prime Minister is a man of his word, and I- know this Parliament will hold him to strict enforcement of that statement. We must have no political management of-that railway, no such management as has disgraced the administration of the Intercolonial Railway system ever since Confederation. I sometimes worry about my good friend the able Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell). I have a good deal of faith in him. During my election campaign in the West I made strong use of his personality; I -spoke about the stern old covenanter that would never strike his colours to the wrong, and yet, when I come down here, I find-and I hope I am not violating any private confidence-that he is not quite sound on this question of railroad management. I excuse him on the ground that he has lived in the Maritime Provinces probably all his lifetime.

speechtext: I just want to put my hon. friend right. More than twenty times during the last fifteen years I have condemned the management of the Intercolonial railway. It is the most unbusinesslike proposition that I have ever known in my life. If the hon. member will look up the pages of Hansard, he will find I have gone further than he will in regard to the management of 'the road in the last twenty-five years.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman quite misunderstood me if he thought for an instant that I was impugning his position on the question.. If he had given me time, I would have excited his delight that I had made the reference. I was only pointing out that while he had lived in Sodom and Gomorrah so long, he had, like Lot seen so much of it that he had become
disgusted with the system and felt that it could never be improved under public ownership.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, he has not.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the Intercolonial Railway has been very badly managed, and he has not scrupled to denounce that management. Of course, it has been badly managed. You could not get anything worse on this side of Hades-if that is a parliamentary term. The whole trouble is this: The Intercolonial Railway was built as a condition of Confederation. When these scattered provinces were formed into Confederation in 1867,. one of the conditions was that a railroad system should be constructed at public expense through the Maritime Provinces, and that it should be linked up with the rest of Canada, at least with Ontario and Quebec. In order, to do that, it was necessary to construct the railway along the coast, touching a village here and there, and this, that and the other town, and it was built, not as ia commercial enterprise, but as a condition of Confederation. Then it remained pretty largely, with an occasional inter-regnum when an effort for improvement was made, in the hands of politicians and under the control of a political department. Need I invite this House to look at the spectacle that was enacted in the last Parliament when the Chief Whip from Nova Scotia threatened to resign because the management, in its best judgment, appointed somebody to a position on that road, and the Whip had not been consulted, and because party considerations had not been paramount, as indeed they have been paramount all these years? Let him resign. We have had, as the Minister of Public Works says, and as everybody who has studied the question knows, about the worst possible mismanagement of the Intercolonial that could be conceived, but it has all been due to political manipulation and control, and that is how my good friend the Minister of Public Works got the idea that public ownership is a failure. The reason why the Intercolonial railway has not been a success is that it has not been managed by business men.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It has been a. failure so far.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Yes, but let mo point this out to the House and to the country that, during most of these years, the freight of the people of the Maritime Provinces has been carried over the Intercolonial railway at about one-third of the

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The railways of the different states have different gauges, and you have to change passenger trains at the boundary lines of the different states.

Air. RICHARDSON;: Just the same as you have different gauges of members in this Parliament, they will cavil at pretty nearly anything you say. But the gauges [DOT]really do not make any difference. Let them standardize their gauges, whether they be large or email, if they choose. I am not referring to gauges here; I am referring to the administration of the system. There is always somebody who can pick a little hole in anything that any one says. Even the great Master, the great law-giver of Nazareth, had holes picked in his utterances, so I do not expect to scape absolutely scot-free in this discussion. I say the system of managing the roads there has *proved a fine success, and if it has proved [DOT]a success in these Australasian colonies, which, of course, are British, why should it not prove an equal success in this great Do-minion, which is also British? I dislike very much to mention the name of 'Germany in this British-Canadian House of Parliament, and yet I am going to state that the railroads in Germany are managed entirely by the State. Do the members of this House know that three-fourths of the people of Germany have travelled for years and years on the German system of railways at a quarter of a cent per mile, while m Canada we pay on an average of three cents per mile, and with the recent addition to rates it may even exceed that? France has public ownership of railroads; so has Austria-Hungary, and so has Italy! and yet we are told even by so good a friend of mine as the Minister of Public Works-he did not actually say it, but I am afraid he sometimes thinks it-that we in Canada have not sufficient inherent honesty in ourselves to manage a Government-owned -system of railroads. I would suppose that on the average we are as honest as the people of other countries, although a great railroad man in this- country once told me that the Canadian people were more dishonest than the .Chinese; he may have been right or wrong, but at all events if we put sufficient guards around ourselves, take away from the Government the power of interfering with the commission, and if we absolutely prevent political manipulation and control, we ought to succeed and surely we can get railway experts like Mr. Shaughnessy-Lord Shaughnessy, I should have said, but as the mover of a resolution to abolish all titles in- this country I -may be forgiven for making that slip-D. -B. Hanna, -Grant Hall, Sir George Bury, and other excellent railway operators now engaged v?ith our big railway systems to work for the country. Surely, if we pro-

tect their positions for them, pay them satisfactory salaries, and give them such assurances that they [DOT]will be satisfied we shall not interfere with them, we can get them to serve us just as they serve the privately-owned roads. I have talked to some of these men as well as many other competent railway operators and I know they would just as readily-some of them have said they would more readily-serve the people of Canada than a private corporation, because most of these men as, indeed, most of our Canadian people, have at heart the idea of service. The average man would like to render service to his country but these men in the past could not be induced to serve publicly-owned roads so long as they were subject? to political manipulation and control, and I do not blame them. But if we adopt the recommendations of the Drayton-Ae-worth report and put our publicly-owned system under the control of a commission of the best available men, and protect that commission from political control, I am satisfied we could get the best railroad .men in the Dominion of Canada to serve us; and well it would be if we could engage such men, because we are bound to embark upon this system, it may not be of our own choosing, but we are nevertheless up against the necessity of embarking on a great publicly-owned system of railways.
In order to make such a system anything like a success, as the Prime Minister said this afternoon, and as I have .already told the House, we shall have to take over certain roads. We have to remember that owing to the absurd competition among these railroad exploiters, subsidy hunters, and manipulators, railroads have been built throughout the country that are entirely unnecessary. Many of you who have travelled over the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern, and the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West know that these roais parallel each other at close range for scores, if not hundreds of miles. Now, if we are to take this great combination of systems over-and we must do so-we must co-ordinate all these roads. We must eliminate every unnecessary mile in the whole system. We must eliminate the mileage that parallels some other road, and in the interests ..f the country we must operate only that mileage that is necessary for serving the people of this country. If we did that, we could probably reduce the mileage of these publicly-owned toads by twenty-five, or thirty. or thirty-five per cent. Then we ' would be face to face with this proposition. The average man may say, "You must
charge rates sufficient to produce interest on the entire capitalization." Are we to charge rates on the Canadian Northern sufficient to produce interest on $528,000,0001 Not so, because we are not going to be able to utilize all that system. We must eliminate at least thirty or thirty-five per cent of the mileage of the roads we take over. Then what must be done? We must strike from the national capitalization at one sweep the entire capital representing the mileage we eliminate. There '? nothing else for it, because in no other way could we make the system pay. If we left the capitalization at the enormous figure which the exploiters would, present to us as the cost of the roads, we could, never pay the operating and maintenance expenses and proper interest on the capital.

speechtext: How are we to eliminate any portion of the $438,000,000 represented by securities?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend in one word-just wipe it off your book.
