speechtext:
That is a pretty easy
way of paying your debts.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
knows that the people of Canada share to some extent in the responsibility for this folly because they supported Governments and parties who did the wrong. It is the people of Canada through their representatives in the provincial legislatures and in this House who have enabled these exploiters to commit this folly. Then let the people of Canada take their loss, as they will be obliged to take their loss. We shall have to wipe off $100,000,000, or $200,000,000, or $250,000,000 from the books, and that is where the iniquity of this bonusing system through all these years to exploiters comes in. But there is only one way to do it. It will just represent that much loss to the people of Canada, and it serves them right because they have gone on conniving at this' thing. They have been warned many times against it, but they have gone on just the same, and the people of Canada will just have to take their loss great as it may he. Then we shall have a publicly-owned system of railroads in this country with a vast mileage capitalized at what the system would have cost to construct under sane conditions. I know of no other way of solving this great question. When you have reduced the capitalization to what it would have been if the system had been constructed under sane and rational conditions, then

and then only can you establish a rate that will be just to the people of this country. I believe that if we co-ordinated these railroads, if we eliminated waste and duplicate mileage, an<^ reduced the capital to proper proportions, we could establish both freight and passenger rates on this nationally-owned system that would produce operating expenses and maintenance charges, as well as a good return on the capital that was actually required to produce the system'; and in my judgment we could have a very much lower rate than we have at the present time.
My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) contrasted the cost of the Canadian Northern Railway system, which he placed at $44,000 per mile, with the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. The cost of the Intercolonial railway, he said, was $65,000 a mile, the cost of the Grand Trunk Pacific was at the rate of $100,000 a mile, and the cost of the Transcontinental railway was at the rate of $90,000 a mile. If you add interest up to the present time on the latter it would increase that cost to $110,000 a mile. In connection with the Transcontinental, I would like to put a question to the members of this committee. Do hon. members recall that, after the completion of the Transcontinental railway, the late Government appointed a commission to inquire into the construction of that road? Do hon. members recall that that commission found and reported that there was $40,000,000 of graft money in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental railway? No wonder the cost of the Transcontinental was run up to $90,000 a mile and $110,000 a mile if you add interest. There were many crimes perpetrated in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. Hon. gentlemen know something of the town of Transcona. If hon. gentlemen go to Transcona they will see something that will almost sicken them of the methods that, were adopted in connection with the manipulation of the townsite terminals and shops there. The town of Transcona is in my riding. I have not time to tell the story, hut there are at that place great shops huilt by the Government led by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, and I understand that those great shops are not being properly operated at the present time. The tragedy of the town of Transcona is one of the iniquities in connection with railway construction in this country. That is a long story and must be told some other 	*
day; I have not time to tell it to-night. In connection with the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, look at the hotels that were built, all at the public expense. It is our money that was used in this folly; it is our money that was used for the construction of these hotels. There is a great hotel in .Edmonton and another in Winnipeg. I saw a report the other day that so great was the loss in the operation of these hotels that the Government contemplate closing them both down.
This country has been on a dreadful spree for the last twenty-five years or more in regard to its railway policy, an orgy that some day will have to be written up. We have had booms in this country and people have been too busy to pay special attention to the great transportation question. As a result these dreadful follies have been committed, and the country is face to face with the consequences and will be obliged to deal with the situation in the
10 p.m sternest fashion. I have observed in this House, within the last few weeks, a feeling of uneasiness on the part of a great many hon. members in regard to the transportation question, and I believe that feeling only reflects- the uneasiness that existsi among the people. No wonder hon, gentlemen have risen in their places day after day and have wanted to know when the Government is going to take control of the 'Canadian Northern! Railway system. No wonder we are anxious to see this road placed in the hands- of an independent board of ekpert railway men, in whose integrity and ability we may have implicit faith. No wonder the country is anxious to see this great system placed under the control of such a board. I believe the people are. beginning to waken up, and to waken up in a lively manner, to the real consequences of the folly that we have been indulging in for the last twenty-five years-. I believe it is because the country is- beginning to waken up that the Government is moving, is ready to acquiesce in, and to comply with, the wishes of the House and the country. It is- because of that feeling in the country that I wish to raise my voice and to bring my influence to bear, to induce the Government to get to this question as rapidly as possible and to find a solution for it. That is the excuse I have for rising in this House as frequently as I have done in connection with this railway situation.
One word in regard to the position which my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) took in

his address this afternoon. He instituted a comparison between the Dominion of Canada and the great Republic to the South. He said he did not believe that three transcontinental lines were too many for Canada because the people of the United States had seven transcontinental lines. I could not help thinking that there i3 no parallel between these two cases. There is this point of difference, however, that the seven transcontinental lines that stretch across the American continent south of the 49th parallel were built almost entirely, except in one or two cases- in which some land assistance was given in the early history of the -country, at the expense of the owners-the stockholders and the bondholders. That is what has happened down there. In addition to that they have a population that enables them to support these seven transcontinental railway lines. But, Mr. Chairman, the three transcontinental railway lines that -cross this North American continent in -Canada were built by the people of 'Canada. The people of the Dominion- have paid dollar for dollar fo,r every foot of railway that has been constructed within the bounds of the country and yet we do not own these railways. We do not need three transcontinental railway lines. I could go on by the hour telling you about the grass and shrubs growing along the line of the Transcontinental and of various portions of that road which are not even being operated. We have tossed $200,000,000 of the people's money into this Transcontinental railway and of what use is it to us at the present time? It has been built a long way ahead of the time when, if ever, it will be required. I believe that if the policy enunciated by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister years ago of contenting ourselves with only one transcontinental railway around the north shore of Lake Superior, to be taken over by the people and left open to all lines to run their trains over, had been adopted we would not have had an expenditure of $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 to face and grapple with at the present critical juncture of the country's history. We would then have had but one Transcontinental road, and what an enormous saving would have been effected in the operation of only one great system. We do not want a lot of railroad corporations. Let me tell hon. members this-and I have it from some of the best railway authorities that ever entered this country-that notwithstanding all that is said to the politicians, all that is said to members of Parliament, and all that is said to the people
of this country about competition, you get no competition, absolutely none. The railroad companies of this country, and of this continent-in fact, the railroads of all countries-are a solid combination. Their officials meet from time to time and fix the rates absolutely between themselves. If one company's line is forty miles longer than another company's line between two given points, those two companies adopt the same tariff, so that there never is competition, and' there never will be competition. So that the thing to-day is to get as many railroads as you can under one management, and if you have them under one management you save so much in staff, so much in salaries, and so much in administration, that it makes an enormous contribution to the success of a railway.
Just a word while it is in my mind with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway. I notice that my hon. friend the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) advocated that the Canadian Pacific should be taken over, and there are some people who say, "Let us take all the railroads over." In my judgment that would be the greatest mistake that -the Canadian people could make in connection with the present solution of the issue. The Canadian Pacific railway is an entity in itself. It is a well-managed corporation-no keener or more efficient management can be found on this continent. But the Government/ system, embracing, as it will embrace, the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island railways, the Transcontinental, and the Grand Trunk Pacific railways, and the old Grand Trunk railway also, will touch practically all important points in the Dominion. What special object would there be in acquiring the Canadian Pacific also? We do not want two lines of railroad touching at the same points; let the Canadian Pacific go on just as it is. But if we take and co-ordinate this great Government system' of railroads, and if we adopt the advice that I have offered with regard to capitalization, I want to assure the House and the country that we shall be able to adopt rates on the Government system that will compel the Canadian Pacific to reduce its present rates, and we shall be doing an inconceiveable service to the people of Canada. Let me illustrate what I mean: We have had -in the city of Winnipeg for the last twenty years or more, a system of electric light and electric power, owned, by the way, by the same interests that control the Canadian Northern. The water power was developed on the Winnipeg river,

and transmitted some sixty or seventy miles into Winnipeg. Six or seven years ago- and it is worth while that every member should know these facts,-the people of Winnipeg, feeling, as they had a right to feel, that the rates they were paying for power and light were much too high, decided to develop a water power and an electric light system.of their own. They procured from the Dominion Government what is known as the Point du Bois Falls on the Winnipeg river, and they developed that system at a cost of six or seven mil-ion dollars. Now, mark you, they cut the rates to one-third of what the people were paying at that time to the Winnipeg Electric Railway interests. Not only that, but they have had a yearly surplus of from $80,000 to $85,000, after providing for sinking fund and all proper expenses of operation for the last two or three years. They have saved, and are saving, the consumers of light and power in the city of Winnipeg $3,000,000 a year, so that in the last six or seven years the total saving to the people of that city has been over $18,000,000, because the other company was obliged to cut its rates and bring them down to the level of the rates charged by the public owned system. In other words, three times the cost of the entire enterprise has been saved to the citizens of Winnipeg. Now, if we adopt the plan proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister, and co-ordinate all these railroads, if we eliminate the useless mileage and wipe out the unnecessary and criminal waste which the public should not have to pay for, I believe we can duplicate	the experience of the
people of Winnipeg and largely reduce the rates that are in force at the present time. Ard the beauty of the proposition is that the great Canadian Pacific Railway, spleudid read that it is, will be obliged to meet our rates, ard then see what a saving the;e will be to the people.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What was the land worth at the time the contract was made?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Never mind what
it was worth; I am telling you what they got out of it. I have not condemned the bargain made; there was a great excuse for it at the time. But I want to explode this absurd notion held bv many
that the Canadian people owe a debt of gratitude to the railroad companies.
Then we gave exemption of duties- on the materials required in the construction of that road, which was a -concession of enormous value at the time. In addition we gave from the public treasury large loans whenever the company asked for them. The time was when it was not the Canadian Northern which was rapping at the doors of Parliament; it was the Canadian *Pacific, and this Parliament always came to the rescue of the Canadian Pacific when it required assistance. Here is something the people of this country perhaps never think of, or have no realization of. We gave the Canadian Pacific exemption from taxation upon all its possessions until Gabriel blows his trumpet. Based on the rate of taxation which exists in the United States, this concession amounts to the appalling approximate sum of $500,000,000 every thirty years. Just think of it. Perhaps you do not recollect all these things, Mr. Chairman, but the exemption from taxation on every dollar's worth that this company owns is worth to them $500,000,000 approximately every thirty years if you take the average rate of taxation prevailing in the United States.
I want to deal with a matter whi-ch I am- sure wiH interest the House. When a company receives, a grant in the old country it is a statutory grant, and a grant toy statute is just as good as if the patents were issued for the land. When the contract was -made in 1881, a clause was- placed in it that:
Notwithstanding any Act of any legislature or ainy municipality all the possessions of the company-
Now -mark this.
-all the possessions of the company, its roadbed, rolling stock, capital stock, station houses and station grounds, shall be exempt from taxation forever
Forever! That is a long time, Mr. Chairman. Now mark what follows:
And the land grant shall be exempt from taxation for twenty years from the grant thereof from the Crown.
It was the understanding of Parliament at the time that while the appurtenances and possessions of the company would be exempt forever, the land1 -grant would -only be exempt from taxation for twenty years from the grant thereof from the Cro-wn. I have explained to the House that when the bargain was ratified, the Government set aside the best agricultural areas through-

out the Northwest, from which the company might select their land grant. But the company did not take out their patents for this land grant at once. I was in Parliament the year before the expiration of this twenty years, and I had learned that the company had not taken out their patents, and had further learned that they proposed to contend that their exemption period should begin with the issue of their patents and not with the statutory grant from the Crown. Learning that, I introduced a Bill in the House of Commons some twenty years ago to interpret that clause. I read from speeches of hon. gentlemen who were in the House of Commons at the time the contract was ratified to show that it was the understanding of Parliament that the exemption of taxation on the land grant should only last for twenty years from the time of the ratification of the contract. I read from the remarks- of Sir Hector Lange-vin, Minister of Public Works in Sir John A. Macdonald's Government. He said:
Therefore in a very short time, the parish or municipality will be settled, and the exemption of taxation on these lands will not be felt, because the land remaining to be sold will remain there only until the settlement can be extended in that direction. So that after the twenty years what will remain exempted from taxation will be just the 100 feet in width on the length of the municipality. [DOT]
It is clear that Sir Hector Langevin understood that the land grant would be taxable in twenty years and that the exemption from taxation would be only the 100 feet of roadbed.
Hon. Edward Blake, the greatest tribune of the people who ever sat in this House, spoke as follows:
They have perpetual exemption-
He was referring to the Canadian Pacific.
from taxation on their enormous property, a monstrous provision, in my opinion; and this monstrosity is not to last merely twenty years, which is the period of bondage in other respects but it is to last forever.
Sir John A. Macdonald, in connection with the ratification of this contract, expressed the view that the Canadian Pacific, owing to the vast subsidies given to it by the people, would be able to carry freight at a very much lower rate-I think he said one-third

than that charged by privately-owned railroads. At that time I introduced an Act to interpret that land-tax exemption clause. I pointed out that the ink was scarcely dry on that contract giving the company a statutory grant of 25,000,000 acres of land when the company borrowed $25,000,000 in land grant bonds, and that [Hr. Richardson.]
the grant was as available for all the purposes of financing of the company as it ever was. But the twenty years expired, and when I introduced an Act to interpret that clause I was met, forsooth, with the most strenuous opposition on the part of leading politicians of this House. I regret to say that the present leader of the Opposition I think at that time, certainly on one occasion-characterized me as a Socialist fcr daring to introduce an Act interpreting a clause in a charter and interfering with vested rights. I. was prompted during my speech in the House by the late Hon. J. G. Haggart, member for Lanark, former -Minister of Railways in Sir John A. Macdonald's Government, and I was able to state to the House that he had introduced an Act for the purpose of interpreting a clause in the Canadian Pacific charter, when it suited the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway company that that interpretation should be made. It happened that they wanted certain remission of duties on material that they had imported, and the Government of the day introduced an Act interpreting a clause in their charter arjd enabling them to make off with a large sum of money. But when I, in my humble capacity as representative of the people, asked that a clause in this charter should be interpreted in order that the interests of the public should be protected, I was denounced as a Socialist. The late Sir Charles Tupper, who was leading the Opposition, also denounced me m the grandiloquent language so characteristic of him, -so that I met with opposition on all sides and was voted down. It was then that I was discovered to be a pestilent fellow, a danger to vested interests, and a menace to the country. As a matter of fact,
I suppose that-I was a menace to the big interests. But-I hope the House will forgive me this personal word-after the next election I was the only member of the entire 213 against whom a petition to unseat was pressed;. All the other protests were sawed off and a conspiracy to drive me from public life was formed by the corrupt manipulators of the two parties who put their heads together to commit the crime.
I had run as an independent candidate in the 1900 election. The Conservatives did not put up a candidate against me and supported me pretty largely. I served one session in that parliament, the protest could not be brought to trial before the House met. At that session I opposed a Bill-a Mackenzie and Mann Bill which was backed by the Conservatives-because I thought it was my duty to do so. That

act of mine was used for my political undoing at that time. The so-called Liberals -that is not Liberalism at all-put up the money, and the Conservative manipulators got the evidence to prove that teams had been hired in my election. Although my entire election expenses were sworn to as being less than $600 in a riding 125 miles long by 100 miles wide, I was unseated, forsooth, on the ground of bribery and corruption. While the judges who sat on that petition were considering their verdict, a bribe was flaunted before them by the "kept" press of that day in the shape of an offer of a seat on the Supreme Court bench of this country for one, and the position of Chief Justice of Manitoba for the other.

But I think the time is past when a conspiracy of that kind can be repeated and carried out successfully. I believe that a better day has dawned in this country. More independence prevails. On this side of the House we have men who belong to different schools of thought, but they speak their minds on public questions with freedom and frankness. What is a free Parliament if it is not a body which giyes to those who sit within it the right to represent the interests of their constituents? subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The point which I
' was making was in connection with the railway question. We have on this side of the House a splendid galaxy of men who are united in seeing that the Government does the best it can with this railway question. I was leading up' to that point, but,
perhaps, having been a partisan in the old days yourself, Mr. Chairman, you may be inclined to a little extent to overlook these things. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the member for North Simcoe has stolen my glass of water. The Minister of Public Works says that my wind is all right; notwithstanding that reminds me of a story. On one occasion the late Hon. George Brown was making a speech in Peterborough. It was very warm; and he was drinking a large quantity of water and was waving his arms about and gesticulating wildly, when an Irishman in the audience said:	" Mr. Chairman, this is the first time that I ever saw a wind-mill run by water."
To conclude that point of my argument abcut the taxation Bill that I was unable to get through the House-I mean my Bill to interpret the tax exemption clause-I think I got six or seven votes to ninety-nine, so that you see the representatives or the " mis-representatives " of the people at that time were pretty solidly lined up with the corporations. We, however, got from' the Government of the day a pledge that they would issue the patents to the railroad companies for their lands, and that they would refer the question to the courts for interpretation as to whether the exemption should date from the ratification of the contracts or from the issue ,of the patents. I pointed out at that time upon the floor of the House that that was a dangerous thing to do; that if the reference were made to the courts of this clause the courts would take cognizance only of the actual wording of the clause, and the last act I performed in Parliament before my undoing 'by virtue of the conspiracy referred to, was to move a resolution that, when the reference was made to the courts, the courts should be requested to take cognizance o.f the understanding of Parliament when the contract was ratified. I think that was a reasonable proposition. My resolution was, however, voted down on that occasion, and the reference was made to the courts-with what result? That the courts did exactly as I predicted they would do; they rendered a decision that the exemption from taxation should bear date from the issue of the patents. Therefore, the Canadian Pacific railway had another twenty years' exemption from taxation on this enormous land grant. Do hon. members realize what this exemption from taxa-. tion has meant and means to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? The other night

I made an estimate that that taxation would be worth, on an average, $2,000,000 a year, and as it runs, or will run, for forty years, if you compound the interest the exemption in that connection alone would probably amount to $100,000,000. About $50,000,000 at least could have been saved to the people of this country if my advice had been taken on that occasion. There is in the Canadian Pacific Railway charter a clause that is known as the ten per cent clause. Let me read it :	'
The Consolidated Railway Act of 1879, respecting tolls, is hereby extended so that such reduction may be to such an extent that such toils when reduced shall not produce less than ten per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in the construction of the railway.
When I was in Parliament in 1896, 1897 and 1898 I was urged by some gentleman in Winnipeg to bring up this question of the ten per cent clause. The company at that time was charging excessive rates in the Northwest- I introduced a resolution that the Government should appoint a commission to find out how much money the country put info the Canadian Pacific and how much money the Canadian Pacific capitalists put in of their own. I made at that time on the floor of the House this argument, which, I believe, is a legitimate one, that in allowing them a profit of ten per cent, we should not allow them ten per cent profit on the tens of millions of dollars that the people put in, but that we should allow them profits only on the money they put in themselves. I need hardly tell the House-it goes without saying-that my resolution was voted down on that occasion by a parliament that seemed to be more considerate of corporations than of public interests. Let me, before I pass from the consideration of the Canadian Pacific, refer very briefly to the position which Lord Shaughnessy, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, took in the manifesto which he issued the other day to the people of Canada, and which was first presented at the annual meeting of that railway company. He said in that statement that those who held the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway had paid on an average of $112 for every $100 of stock. When I read that statement, my memory carried me back to the first issue of stock of $20,000,000 which was distributed during the * construction of the road amongst members of the syndicate and their associates at twenty-five per cent of its par value. This twenty million dollars worth of stock realized five million dollars, and this lat-

ter amount was set aside and was paid back to the purchasers of the stock in dividends at the rate of six per cent per. annum par value, so that in four years they .got back their own money and they owned the stock besides. That is pretty good 'financing. In 1883, also before the road was completed, there was another issue of thirty million dollars' worth of stock distributed amongst the members of the syndicate, shareholders and friends, at fifty cents on the dollar. Therefore, out of the first fifty million dollars of stock the company realized only twenty million dollars in capital, cash. This stock was also a paying investment for the shareholders, because even before the road was built, they received their six per cent per annum par value, and they soon received back more than they had paid for the stock, and they owned the stock besides. If hon. members have any desire to make fuller investigation and to check the figures I have given, they might look up the sessional papers of the day.
In addition to the aid granted to the Canadian Pacific railway, which I have already stated, over thirty million dollars were contributed to subsidiary companies. Provincial Governments granted to subsidiary companies of the Canadian Pacific railway twelve million dollars; British Columbia contributed 6,389,000 acres of land, which has netted the company an enormous amount of money, and they still own over 11,000,000 acres. They have realized from the sale of lands and townsites nearly $124,000,000, exclusive of the lands which the company still hoilds, and which cannot be worth less than $115,000,000 or $120,000,000. That makes a total public assistance to the company of $228,500,000. Then if you add $400,000,000 of the value of the taxation exemption, exclusive of land tax exemption for the thirty-five years the company has been in existence, it will bring the public aid up to the appalling sum of $628,000,000. If you add to that $125,000,000 for land, townsites, etc., already unsold, you have the surprising approximate figure of $753,000,000, which almost approaches the valuation that Lord Shaughnessy, in his recent manifesto, places upon the assets of the company to-day; which manifesto was, I think, issued for the purpose of serving notice on the Canadian people that if they nationalize the Canadian Pacific railway they must pay an enormous figure for it. I think the House will agree with me that the Canadian people are' not under any very profound debt of gratitude, as some

would have us think, to the great Canadian Pacific Railway corporation.
I do not want, to go into the figures of the aid given by the country to the Canadian Northern railway. We have had those figures almost ad nauseam. The Prime Minister, this afternoon, in his able resume, gave to the House most comprehensive figures. I have already, earlier in the evening, dealt with that aspect of affairs.
Let us now take up the question of the Grand Trunk railway. It was in the early days when the old Grand Trunk railway was established in this country, and the union between politics and the railway corporations does not seem to have been as close or as direct as it developed later on. The total subsidies to the old Grand Trunk railway were thirteen million dollars. Many years ago the Government loaned this company fifteen million dollars which were never repaid, and this makes a total of twenty-eight million dollars. If you add these two sums and figure out compound interest upon them for the long period, the result will be a huge sum.
I promised earlier in the evening to make some reference to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or Transcontinental line. The construction of this enterprise is perhaps the most insane upon which the Canadian people ever embarked. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, coupled with others in and out of the House who surrounded him in 1903, are responsible for this monstrosity. If time permitted, I should like to deal fully with the history of this enterprise, but it is not of such distant date that the country is not perhaps pretty well .seized of the facts. In launching the project in Parliament, the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who was then Prime Minister, spoke as follows:
It is not of to-morrow, but of this day, of this hour and of this minute. Heaven grant that it be not already too late; Heaven grant that whilst we tarry and dispute, the trade of Canada is not deviated1 to other channels.
Let me recall to the House, the reply which the late Hon. Mr. Blair, who at that time was Minister of Railways in the Laurier Cabinet, made to the right hon. gentleman. Here are Mr. Blair's words:
What does the right honourable gentleman mean when he says: "The flood of tide is upon hs that leads us on to fortune; if we let it pass, it may never recur again"? What does the right hon. gentleman mean when he says: "If we let it pass, the voyage of our National life, bright as it is to-day, will be bound in shallows?" What does the right hon. gentleman mean when he says: "We cannot wait, because time does not wait?" I think, Mr. Speaker, and I say it with all respect to my right hon. friend, that it would have been as correct if not so poetic, for him to have said:

" We cannot wait, because Senator Cox cannot wait."
I shall not go further 'into the history of the inception of this enterprise. I would recommend h-on. members to read up Hansard of that interesting period and learn what was said on the floor of the House about this preposterous proposition.
I want to repeat the point I made earlier in my remarks, that I do not believe anything is to be gained by indulging in recriminations with regard to the responsibility of this or that party for the condition cf affairs we find at the present time.
, As 1 have already said, all parties are almost equally responsible, and the best thing we can do is to get behind the right ' hon. leader of the Government in endeavouring to evolve a satisfactory national stale-owned system out of the roads that must in a very short time come to us, and some have already come. I believe that that object can be accomplished very much more easily by a Union Government than I believe that the country-is seized of the seriousness of the situation, and I believe seriousness of the situation, and I believe the Government also notwithstanding the stress of work due to its multitudinous and exacting duties also realizes how serious the situation is. 1 believe the speech which the right hon. Prime Minister delivered this afternoon must have convinced the country, as it certainly convinced members of this House, that he at least is fully seized of the importance of the whole question, and that he and his Government propose to solve that problem in the near future in a manner that I trust will redound to the interest and credit of the country. I should like to see the Canadian state-owned system of railways placed at as early a date as possible in the hands of such a management as was foreshadowed by the Prime Minister this afternoon and as recommended in the Drayton-Acworth report. I believe the importance of the question necessitates the earliest possible solution. Speaking for myself, I am very much gratified to find that the Government as represented here this afternoon in the very able deliverance by the Prime Minister is fully alive to the importance of the whole question and has resolved to apply the solution at the earliest possible date.

speechtext:
B. NICHOLSON: At this late hour and at a time when we are all anxious to conclude the work of the session and get away as soon as possible, I would hesitate



to rise and say anything on this question but for the fact that I feel, like the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, that this is one of the burning questions before the people of this country, and one to which we should all at least endeavour to direct some attention in order that the best possible solution may be found of the railway problem in this country. If I were to follow the remarks of my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) I would be compelled to disagree with many of the arguments' he advanced and with many of the conclusions he reached. But it is not my purpose to deal with his remarks. I (wish to direct my attention to what the actual condition is with regard to the whole railway situation in this coun-[DOT] try and see if I can offer any suggestions that will assist in finding a possible solution. In passing, I might 6ay that I entirely disagree with the gloomy picture my hon. friend from Springfield drew of the future of this country when he left it to be understood that in his opinion the development of this country would never be s-ich as to make necessary the railways we now have projected from one end of the country to the other. I heartily agree with what was said in that connection by the right hon. leader of the Opposition this afternoon, because I believe the time will come, and come very shortly, when three transcontinental lines, properly equipped and operated, will be required to handle the traffic of this country. These roads may have been projected a little too soon, but let me point out this: In the United States they have a population of four hundred people to every mile of railway, whereas in Canada, according to the last census, we have only one hundred and eighty-five people to each mile of railway. Now, in order to bring our population, sparse a6 it is, up to the same standard in relation to railway mileage as prevails in the United States, we need to increase our poulation just up to sixteen million people, and I do not think it is a very far cry to the day when we shall have sixteen million people in this country. I am assuming for the moment that our railway mileage should be proportionate to our population, but when we remember that our population is spread over an area as large as the United States, I think the argument will not hold water that population proportionate to railway mileage is a fair way of determining what our mileage should be. I would point out to- the hon, -member for Springfield that whereas in 1896 the gross earn-
ings of all the railways in Canada serving the territory now being served by the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental was $38,000,000. in 1916, or just twenty years later, they had increased to $160,130,786. I would also like to remind my hon. friend that I had the privilege of running a locomotive on one of these transcontinental railways during the year when the first 1,000,000 bushels of wheat was hauled over the Canadian Pacific, then the only transcontinental railway in existence from the head of the lakes to the seaboard. In the first year when they hauled that 1,000,000 bushels of wheat it was an event in the history of this country. During this last winter 1,000,000 bushels of wheat was moved out of Fort William in one single day. If we had had the facilities to carry the traffic there would have been two or three million bushels of wheat being moved daily at some periods during the winter just passed. I have read a statement by a gentleman, who takes a position very similar to that of the hon. member for . Springfield in regard to this question, that there have been wheat and flour stored in the West for years because there have not been railway facilities to get it out. I do [DOT] not believe that is so, but it is just an evidence of the extreme statements that men will make when they undertake to bolster up a position that requires an extreme statement to support it.
I would like to refer to the position of the railways in this country with regard to what they have cost and what they must earn. The value of a railway property can only be estimated, providing it has been projected with a reasonable degree of common sense and properly -built-, o-n the basis of its mileage cost. We have in Canada approximately 40,000 miles of railway and in connection with these railways the Canadian people have paid $-956,085,581, exclusive of the Intercolonial railway. The Prime Minister gave ns .some figures with regard to the Intercolonial this afternoon and placed'the total investment in that road at $137,184,199.62. My own opinion is that it would be difficult to find a group of chartered accountants in the country who could determine what the Intercolonial has cost this country, if you figured it out on the same -basis as that on which any private institution would figure it out. The question is.: What have we got for the expenditure of this money? Let us take the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian

Pacific, the Transcontinental, the Grand Trank Pacific and the Canadian Northern, dealing with each separately.
The Canadian Pacific is the most complete, most efficient and the most economically operated railway system in the world. I wonder whether my hon. friend from [DOT]Springfield knows that it is part of the system of railways that gives the cheapest transportation that is given anywhere in the civilized world? The Australian railways were referred to as an example of the success that may be made in
11 p.m. the operation of publicly owned railways, and the question was asked if they could do that in Australia why could not we do it in Canada? It costs the people of Australia two cents per ton mile for every ton of freight that is moved while it costs the people of Canada three-quarters of a cent per ton mile for every ton of freight that is moved. That shows how successful they are in the operation of state railways in Australia. If you refer to . the Drayton^Acworth report you will see that that is the system of railways that is held up by all those who advocate public ownership of railways as the best and most economically operated system of railroads in the world.

the Canadian Northern, a considerable amount of valuable assets. They have grain elevators at the head of the lakes, capable of taking care of 10,000,000 bushels,; they have six lake steamers plying on the Great Lakes; there are the' Canadian Northern Telegraph and the Great Northwestern Telegraph companies with 1,500 offices; and a variety of subsidiary assets which go with a railway of that character. Let me repeat again:	you can investigate conditions as
you will, and if you can find another railway on the American continent brought up to that standard at a cost of $60,000 a mile, you will have found something that I have been unable to get any information of. My honourable friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) this evening referred to the Canadian Pacific as having cost $46,000 per mile, and he used one set of figures given Out by the President of the Canadian Pacific in the last annual statement ; but he entirely overlooked in the same statement what was given as the total cost of the road. The cost of the Canadian Pacific, including $131,000,000 of earnings put back into betterments and equipment, was $818,000,000, or $61,000 per mile for the whole system just as it is. No, the figures I have given will not double-track the Canadian iNorthem, but will put that road and its equipment on a basis equal to what the Canadian Pacific is on. And it will cost the 'Canadian Pacific $10,000,000 to get its grades between Port Arthur and Sudbury equal to those of the Canadian Northern between the same points. I know what I am talking about, because I have been over both lines; and T know what the Canadian Pacific is figuring on in connection with that line.
A great deal has been said with regard to what the Canadian people have put into the Canadian Pacific and what the Canadian Pacific shareholders have put into it. If we were to judge by the remarks of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) we would come to the conclusion that the Canadian people had built the Canadian Pacific railway and presented the shareholders with many hundreds of millions of dollars in addition. You can investigate the figures from top to bottom if you will, and you will find that what the Canadian Pacific has received by way of cash sub-
sidies and cash from their land grant, and the completed road that was given to them when they started, at a value of about $30,000,000, is $200,000,000 or $14,000 per mile on the total mileage of the road. The old Grand Trunk, which is supposed not to have received anything from the Canadian people, received more than $8,000 per mile as a cash bonus on the total mileage of their railway. speechtext:
1916. The Canadian Pacific is earning $9,593 per mile on every mile. The balance in favour of the Grand Trunk is $1,390 per mile. The Grand Trunk earnings on the Canadian Pacific railway mileage basis would have been reduced by $4,630,090. The Canadian Pacific earnings on the Grand Trunk mileage basis would have been increased by $18,070,000. However, that is beside the point; the question we have to consider is how are we going to deal with this combination of railways and get an efficient transportation system economically operated -with reasonable freight rates. Three proposals have been submitted, one of which is the nationalizing of all Canadian railways. I am opposed in principle to the nationalization of railways, because I do not believe that you can do with the biggest things in the country what you cannot* do with the little ' things. While there is no other way out of it; while we have to make the best of the situation, the solution of the whole problem >if it were possible, would he our getting back to the position we were in fifteen years ago and putting the railways into the hands of privately-owned companies under proper regulations.
It has also been suggested->-in fact the Drayton-Acworth report contains this recommendation-that all the roads be iurned

over to one large private company. I have prepared a group of figures to show what would be necessary both in the case of the present owners continuing as they are and in the case of a new corporation being formed to take over the entire group of railways. If the .Grand Trunk undertook to continue and the sum of $100,000,000 were written off the National Transcontinental to cover the moneys squandered in the enterprise, they would still have to assume ai present liability of $852,416,697 and in addition would have to find at least $100,000,000 in cash to put the system in a position to make even partial operation a possibility. They would continue to be handicapped by lack of traffic-gathering branches throughout the entire 'Canadian West. If the Canadian Northern railway undertook to carry their obligations, they would assume a liability of $400,000,000 and have to find in addition at least $150,000,000 in cash to make the operation of their system possible. If the two were combined in one group or company, as is suggested in the Drayton-Acworth report, the amount of $1,252,416,697 would have to be found, and, eliminating all necessary obligations, at least $150,000,000 to $175,000,000 would have to be furnished for equipment and betterments to put the roads in a position . to make their successful operation a possibility. In other words, the total liabilities of the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the National Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern, assuming that the Canadian people wrote off $100,000,000 for what has been wasted in the Transcontinental, would be. $1,252,416,697.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Canadian people borrowed a certain amount of money and put it into the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. For all practical purposes, they might as well have thrown it into lake Superior. When you come down to operate these railways as a business proposition, the liabilities which I have mentioned will be simply charged to the national debt and the people will pay interest on it, not because they put it into a railway, but because they permitted a group of grafters to get away with it. We are trying to get our railways down to a point where they can be operated as a business proposition, and we have to- bring the capitalization down to a mileage basis in proportion to that of competing lines and to what the actual cost of the railway should be. It is not fair to ask the people who are paiying freight and passenger rates on Canadian railways to pay interest on money that we . deliberately threw away. Take, for instance, the case of the Grand Trunk proper, with liabilities amounting to $475,000,000. The Drayton-Acworth report, page 12, gives as the amount of securities outstanding against the 3,331 miles of the Grand Trunk as $424,169,310, and their experts say that they must have $51,000,000 in order to bring the equipment of the road up to standard. It is my opinion that $51,000,000 will not furnish the necessary equipment.
