speechtext: Is it not a fact that, although the Grand Trunk had a greater number of locomotives than the other railways, those locomotives were so old that the drawbar efficiency made them practically inefficient for operating purposes?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That may possibly be so, at least to some degree, hut to my mind it is worth while finding out just where all those locomotives are.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: In the shops.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Some of them may be in the shops, but information brought to me indirectly is that they are not all in the shops. The Grand; Trunk is operating railroads both in Canada and the United States, and my information is that the Grand Trunk in Canada has been robbed for the benefit of the Grand Trunk m the United States. That may or may not be, but it is a matter at least worth investigating. There is another point in connection with that. My hon. friend has said that the reason for the Grand Trunk
difficulty is that their locomotives are obsolete. I shall give the Minister of Railways and Canals a thought in this connection.
Who is it who is designing the locomotives the Canadian Government is purchasing for the Grand Trunk railway? My reason for asking is this: The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has referred to the fact that the Grand Trunk locomotives are obsolete. I may tell' him that the Grand Trunk put new locomotives built by the Canadian Locomotive Company at Kingston into service less than three years ago, that were obsolete before they were turned out of the shops; positively obsolete, because they were of a type and cflass that was discarded twenty years ago by every railway using the modern locomotives. So, if we are purchasing locomotives for the Grand Trunk railway I would say to the Minister of Railways, be sure and find out who is designing them.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. member agrees with me that the locomotives being built for the Grand Trunk have not sufficient draw-bar efficiency to make them up to date, that the designing is bad, that the engineering service is not as it should be.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
A locomotive may be obsolete and still have draw-bar efficiency. When I referred to a type of locomotive that was obsolete twenty years ago I was not referring to, the draw-bar capacity of the locomotive, but to what it is going to cost to keep that locomotive in a state of efficiency on the road. I repeat that the last locomotive built for the Grand Trunk that I have had the privilege of seeing-and I make a business of watching for all these things-was of a type that was obsolete twenty years ago.
Now a word as to the Canadian. Northern and its equipment. The road is not fully equipped, but from one end of the road to the other what they have got is all modern equipment, and it is due to the fact that they have modern officials, and if the Minister of Railways is purchasing engines there is one man I know of who can. give him sound advice, namely, the General Manager of the Canadian Northern lines east of Port Arthur.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Air. Vaughan?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No, but a gentleman who learned his business with Air. Vaughan. I ain giving that information because I think the Government should know it. It is only by getting down to details that we shall ever get out of what

the hon. member for Springfield terms " this mess," and that is what I have endeavoured to do in a rambling sort,of way to-night. There is one other matter I want to refer to, and that is how we are going to manage these railways, and the tolls we are going to exact when we do manage them. I have studied the question from every angle, and if the declaration of the Prime Minister means anything, and I am one of those who believe it means just exactly what he said, I can see no better way than to follow the plan outlined in the DraytonrAcworth report. It will be absolutely necessary for the Canadian Parliament or the Canadian Government to appoint the first board of directors, but if the board is to be kept out of politics it should be self-perpetuating, in just the same way that the board of directors of any private-owned railway in Canada is self-perpetuating. I believe hon. gentlemen will agree with me that should the president of the Canadian Pacific retire, or before he retires for that matter, he will practically nominate his own successor, and the man he choses will be accepted by the directors, and the shareholders will back him up, and unless we are to have a new group of political directors for the State-owned system of railways in Canada, every time a change occurs we must find some means of having the members of the board chosen without coming back to Governments and Parliaments, because Governments and Parliaments will always be political so long as they exist.
Mr. MeMASTER: If my hon. friend's suggestion is carried out, how will the railways owned by the people of Canada be controlled in any way by the people of Canada?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER AS TO THE CONTEMPLATED POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Place them
under the Railway Commission, as far as control is concerned. As I understand it, the Drayton-Acworth report recommends that the power of nomination should rest with what they term the Dominion Railway Company, but I would term it a board of trustees for the Canadian people. The power of confirmation should rest with the Canadian Parliament or the Canadian Government. That is my idea. If \ some one else can suggest a better, all right, get busy. If we will look at what the Drayton-Acworth report refers to as the most efficient system of government-owned railways in the world, the Australasian experiment, we shall find that they have been changing from commission to board and then back again to commission, back and forth all the time, just because of political appointments. I

say- that if we are going to have political appointments in the operation of a state-owned system of railways, our last condition will be very much worse than the first.
The rates charged on the Government railways should be under the same control as the rates of privately-owned railways. I should like to refer for a moment to something that has been said with regard to the increase of rates granted Canadian railways by the Railway Commission a short time ago. The Government has been severely criticised for not reversing the order of the Railway Commission, but in my judgment if the Government is deserving of censure at all, it is because they took that order of the Railway Commission under consideration even in the slightest degree, and for this reason:	If we are going to have independent control of railways, we cannot possibly set up the principle that every ruling of the Railway Commission is going to be revised by the Government of the day. Reverse the position for a moment, and assume that the Railway Commission orders a reduction of freight rates. Would that be a matter for the Government to revise? Should the Government say the reduction must not take place? The one is just as logical as the other,, and it just comes down to this. I take it that we regard the Railway Commission as we would a court of justice in this country, and I do not think there is a man who would suggest that after a court had given its decision the -case should go for review before a political body. Now as to the merits of the case. The railway companies have to earn increased salaries and an increased cost of all their materials, and I do not think that an increase of fifteen per cent was a large increase in proportion to the increased price they have to pay for everything. The difficulty is that people get a wrong view of what is essential and what is not essential. There are many in this House, for instance, who would say that the railways are not an agency for the production of anything, that they simply stand as a bar between producer and consumer. Now if some of the gentlemen representing a constituency in the West, we will say, will come with me one day next winter and get off the passenger train at White River I will undertake to get him a pass to ride on one of the 210 per cent engines running from White River to Chapleau. I will not ask him to handle a scoopful of coal the whole way, but just keep warm if he can and watch the men who are marketing the farmers' wheat, and I think at the end of the ride he will have a different con-

oeption of what production and consumption really mean. The hon. member for Springfield, speaking on this question a few nights ago, said with all the dramatic eloquence of which he is capable that the tragedy of the increase in the. freight rates was not that the freight rates were increased by fifteen per cent, but that on the very day the order went into effect the price of sugar in the West went up one-tenth of one cent per pound. Would he believe that the locomotive fireman who helps to market the western farmers' wheat found that on the day that the wheat commission set the price of wheat 180 per cent higher than it was in pre-war days his wife had to pay 125 per cent more for the bread to make the sandwiches that she put up in his .lunch basket? I have not heard anybody say that there was any tragedy' about that. I have heard people undertake to say that the price of wheat went up too high but I could not agree with them. I believe it was the right thing for the commission to do in order that they might induce greater production of the things necessary to feed the people during the war. I have also heard it said in business circles that, because the price of newsprint. paper went up fifty per cent it was no reason why the daily newspapers should have increased the prices in their job printing departments 200 and 300 per cent. I do not agree with that. I am just repeating these statements but they do not represent my own views. I do not agree with 'the callous-hearted people who make these statements, and the only reason I refer to them is that I believe that when the hon. member undertakes to stage a tragedy based on the fact that one-tenth of a cent a pound has been added to the price of sugar he should at least exercise some little regard in the selection of the costume that the villain is going to appear in. To come back to the main question. Whatever is done with the Canadian railways, one thing that is necessary, if we are going to have efficiency and economy, is to find some means of keeping the overhead charges down to a proper basis and putting the .railways in the hands of men who will operate them independently of any political considerations whatever and just the same as a private company would operate its own railway.
Mr. MANI'ON:	The hon. gentleman
speaks about the Australian railways; what about the German, Belgian, French and Swiss State-owned railways?

I stated that I would make no comparison between the
railways of Central Europe and the railways on the North American continent for the reason that it is utterly impossible. A railway must earn a sufficient amount of money to pay for the things it uses. We cannot make any comparison between conditions in Canada and those on the European continent. You can produce anything you like to mention in Central Europe a great deal, cheaper than you can, produce it in Canada. We are not going to ask our people to work for what the people of Europe get. I simply used the Australian railways for the purposes of comparison because the Drayton-Acworth report pointed them out as examples of Government ownership.

At this late hour I have only a few observations to make and I shall try to confine myself to about fifteen minutes. I have taken a good deal of interest in the railway question and as I listened to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) presenting the case in regard to the Canadian Northern I felt that it was one of the most masterly expositions of the financial side of the railway question that I had ever heard in this House since I have had the honour of a seat in it. The railway situation certainly does not present a rosy appearance. But, in the meantime we must view these things as they are and not as we would like to see them. Both political parties have gone very far astray on this railway business. A third transcontinental railway should never have been built in this country for at least fifty years. But we went into it with our eyes open, or at least a large part of the people did. The first election that I went into as a candidate for this House I won in opposition to the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental railway. I got a very narrow majority, it is true, but I fought the election on that issue and I am thankful to-day to be able to say that I was opposed to this project from its inception. I looked upon it as a waste of money. But it went on and the cost has assumed proportions that were never dreamed of in those days. But, we cannot now go back upon it. We are involved in the expenditure, the money has been spent and we have to make the best of the situation. It has, to say the least of it, imposed a staggering, colossal indebtedness upon the people of Canada. The war is looked upon as a tremendous enterprise, and so it is, but my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has shown that in order to nationalize the railways

of Canada we would have to pay practically tw^e as much as we have spent in the war, or twice $1,000,000,000. I think my hon. friend placed the total railway capitalization of the country at
12 p.m. $2,500,000,000. At all events, that is within the mark. It will cost $2,500,000,000 to take possession of all the railways in Canada and to provide for the indebtedness in connection therewith. One thing I give my hon. friend great credit for ;s the statement with regard to the financial position of the railways of Canada which he has placed on Hansard to-night. I think he must be a practical railway man. I have received a great deal of information from the splendid address which he has given. It stands out it- striking contrast to the speech delivered from this side of the House by the hon. gentleman who preceded him. I think the statements placed upon Hansard by the hoc. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) are the most lamentable I have neard made in this House on any great question. My main reason ior rising to-night was to try and say a few words to combat what has been placed in Hansard by the hon. member for Springfield. If that hon. gentleman knew one-tenth as much about railways as he thinks he does I should not have spoken to-night, but I feel convinced that the bulk of what he has placed on Hansard will not bear inspection on the part of any business man as being a fair statement of the railway situation.
The Prime Minister has informed us that the Canadian Northern railway has a total 1' ability of $438,000,000. It is said to be worth, according to the figures the Prime Minister gave us, $518,000,000; so that it should have a balance on the right side of about $80,000,000. Of the two propositions, the 'Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, the chances of the former paying are one hundred-fold better than the latter, in my judgment, My hon. friend from East Algoma has shown that it has the lowest capitalization per mile of any railway upon this continent. That is something in its favour. Of course, it is not up to standard. We admit that. My hon. friend has submitted figures showing that $60,000 per mile will bring it up to standard whereas up to the present it has cost -about $45,000 per mile.
It is admitted by all who know the railways of Canada that the best-placed railway, as far as the West is concerned, is the Canadian Northern with its branches. In saying that I am not saying anything
[Mr. Cockshutt. 1
disrespectful of the Canadian Pacific. The first speech I ever made in my public life was in favour of the building of the Canadian Pacific and carrying out the bargain that we had entered into at Confederation- because it must not be lost sight of that the Canadian Pacific was built to redeem the promise made at Confederation that we should link up with British Columbia. That was a bargain just as much as the Intercolonial was a bargain with the people of the East and that must always be borne in mind. The hon. member for Springfield asserted that we paid far more out of the coffets of the Dominion than we -should have paid for the Canadian Pacific. I am not going into that; it is ancient history. But, I do not agree with him in that. We have the finest transportation system in the world, bar none, in the Canadian Pacific. All honour to the men who put it through, all honour to the men who conceived the idea and successfully built that road, and all honour to the present management who are administering it with an .efficiency that few railways in the world have attained.
But we have to face the position as we find it to-day, and the Canadi-an Northern railway is being taken over by the Government, I know that many hon. members, are very impatient because the road is not already administered by the Government, or by some commission appointed by the Government. But we must wait a little, the value of -the stock has still to be adjudicated upon in the courts. You cannot take possession until the price is settled- not very well, or if you do you will be operating at a disadvantage and be liable to further trouble, taking possession of the road before the value is settled. We do know that the $60,000,000 of stock will not cost more than- ($10,000,000-that is the limit set. Now there are a great many people who say, "That is all absurd. We need not have paid a dollar. There has been too much money put into that road already by the people, and therefore we should take possession of it without giving those who own the stock -the slightest advantage in the way of an arbitration-let us just expropriate that stock and take possession*'. That would be a high-handed piece of business, which, in my judgment, would not be at all right. I want to tell the members of the House that -a railroad, the same as- any other property, is always worth the amount it would fetch under the hammer, -at any rate. We have in this country a tremendous railway in the Canadian Pacific. All honour to it, and all

credit, as I have said, for the way it is managed. But I am here to speak as a member of this House, and believing that I speak the feelings of the people of a large part of Canada from east tc, west and from north to south, after having put as much money into railways as we have done, we do not wish to see the whole of our Dominion placed in the hands of one railway company. That is what would have happened in Canada if the Canadian Northern railway had gone under the hammer: There was only one possible buyer of that road in the Dominion and tnat w&s the Canadian Pacific railway, who were anxious to obtain it and would have obtained it, I believe, if that course had been taken. Then the people of. Canada would have shouted, and they would have had a good right to shout, because, after having built three transcontinental lines we are not prepared to put them into the hands of one railway company and have no competition, after all the money that we have spent. Let that never be lost sight of-we could not afford to do that. Even if we lost money in taking the Canadian Northern railway over, I believe when the position is explained thoroughly to the people of Canada, they will say that the Government is right, and that we could not afford to let that system pass into the hands of the Canadian Pacific, as in my judgment, it would undoubtedly have done if it had gone under the hammer. Now that is a point that I think ought to be thoroughly emphasized. We want railway competition in Canada, the West particularly is absolutely set upon competition, and that is the reason, in my judgment-one of the main reasons, at all events- why the Government has taken the course it has and is keeping the Canadian Northern railway as a separate entity and to be run as a separate entity, either by the Government or by a commission.
I myself believe that it is possible, even with the black outlook of the tremendous expenditure that has to be incurred in. connection with the railway situation, to make the railways of Canada still pay a fair dividend upon all the money that has gone into them. It is a big proposition, but I believe it ultimately can be done. Let us look at the situation for a moment. My honorable friend (Mr. Nicholson) who has just spoken has shown you that we are carrying freight, if I remember his figures rightly, at three-quarters of a cent per ton per mile-I think that was his statement. Despite our rigorous climate, despite the tremendous force that we must exert in
winter to run our railways at all, there is no country in the world-barring only the United States, and that country only in certain sections-that has as cheap freight rates as we have in the Dominion at the present time. That is something we ought to recognize, it is something to be proud of, and I think that the administration of our railways has shown that we are prepared to carry freight in a rigorous climate, where the temperature in the winter season goes down to twenty, thirty, forty and even fifty degrees below zero, and there are snowfalls anywhere from five to ten feet deep in our northern country that have to be pushed out of the way-and still in spite of all that we are carrying freights at an infinitesimal rate per mile as compared with the old countries of Europe that have as much population to the square mile as we have in a hundred square miles. We hear a great deal about the splendid administration of European . railways.
I have crossed the Atlantic nearly fifty times, and I have travelled on most of the railways in Europe many and many a time, and there is not a country in the world, in my judgment, that carries passengers in as much comfort, and in as reasonable a way, as do the railways in the Dominion of Canada and in the United States. My honourable friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) told us that people travel at a quarter of a cent, I think it was, per mile in Germany. He has more knowledge of Germany than I have if he can make that statement truthfully. I have travelled a great deal in Germany myself, I have visited that country five or ten times, and my experience was that not only did I not travel for a quarter of a cent per mile,, but that it cost me a great deal more per mile to travel than it does on any of the railways of Canada. That was my experience, and if there are any other gentlemen here who have travelled much I think they can state also that they have never travelled in any country in Europe at any such charge as the honourable gentleman has spoken of, it is absurd on the face of it. Nobody who has travelled in Europe can tell me that. People have never been able to buy railway tickets from Cook, Son & Co., who aTe supposed to have the lowest rates that any firm in Europe have for travelling for any ' such price as the honourable member has spoken of.

I think in justice to the honourable member for Springfield it should be stated that in the European

countries-particularly in Germany and Belgium-they have special rates for working men going to and from their work that are very low. I think the honourable gentleman is absolutely right in regard to the ordinary rates of travel, for first:class passage, and so forth, but for the average workingman there are exceedingly low rates in Germany and Belgium.

I am very much
obliged to my honourable friend for making that statement. I do not wish to mis-state the position of the honourable member for Springfield, who is not in the House at present. I believe there are tickets sold at low rates that enable you to travel as much as you like between certain points. I know such tickets are issued-that you can get a passbook for thirty days, and that you can travel as much on the road as you like between certain points- but a man is not going to travel any more than he feels necessary, and under those circumstances the rate does not work out at as low a rate as might be looked for. I am speaking of the general rates that would be charged to passengers when travelling, not for a little distance that a workman would have to go between his home and his place of work, and which I do not think is a fair comparison. Certainly I was misled and others were misled listening to the figures given by the hon. member for Springfield to-night.
Some considerable attention has been given to Australia as an example. I have had the privilege of also visiting Australia, but I am not sure that the hon. member for Springfield has visited that country. I can speak candidly of the railway service rendered throughout Australia and the accommodation given, because I was there a few years ago. What did I find? At every boundary line between states you had to get out of bed at night if you were sleeping in a Pullman, and change to . another Pullman, and every state has a different gauge on its roads. The remark was interjected that I was a narrow-gauge man when I asked a question during the hon. member for Springfield's speech, but I would draw that hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that in Australia every state has a different gauge practically on its railways. Moreover, they have to transfer all the freight at these state boundaries, from one car to another. The reason for that is that the labour men say that more labour is rendered necessary than there would be if they only had the one gauge, and they

want the system continued. Therefore, freight is transferred from one car to another at the present time on the state boundary line.

Are those railways
operated by the Government?

They are stateoperated. These railways were mostly ibuilt by the States before the Commonwealth came into effect. The Confmonwealth has been in existence now upwards of ten years, and up to the time I visited Australia they had not made any attempt to standardize their gauges. When I asked: "How can you possibly continue to have all the passengers change at your state boundaries, and to tranship all your freight from one car to another," they saidi: "Well, we have a large element here upon the railways who say we would be destroying their means of obtaining a livelihood if we allowed these cars to run through; that is why we have not made our gauges uniform." All the rates in Australia are infinitely higher than ours both as to freight and as to passengers, unless they have lately come down, and their cost per mile is infinitely more than ours. So I think the comparison between Australia and Canada does not work out to our disadvantage. I mention this to show that we are not so badly off as we have been made out to be. We are in a better position than many countries considered to be . as bad as we are at the present' time. I admit that some of the roads are unnecessary duplications. But I am sorry I cannot quite agree with my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), when he said that the road between Toronto and Napanee should be ripped up. As one who travels frequently between Torontq and Ottawa, I find the Canadian Northern a tremendous advantage, and to rip that line up would be to say that you will have no alternative route from Toronto to Ottawa. It must be remembered that the Grand Trunk does not run into Ottawa from Toronto, unless you go down to Coteau Junction, which is only about thirty miles from Montreal, and which is a most round about way to reach Ottawa. The capital of the Dominion had only one road from Toronto until the Cana-' dian Northern came in. This road, in my opinion, is serving a very valuable purpose in Ontario.
I want to dwell for a moment or two upon the position of the Canadian Northern, relative to the traffic that can be obtained by it. I had the pleasure not two years ago of travelling from one end of that road

to the other. I would not say that it has the best roadbed in the Dominion, but we travelled comfortably from Toronto to Vancouver at the rate of twenty-five miles per hour without .mishap, and the engine was able to haul twelve to fourteen heavily-laden cars over the whole of the road. If I remember correctly it hauled fourteen cars, certainly not less than twelve heavily-laden Pullman cars over the Rocky Mountains. That is something which could not be done, I believe, on any other railway either to the north or to the south of the international boundary. I believe the Canadian Northern has the best grade of any of the roads, and the Grand Trunk Pacific runs over a part of the same tracks. One hon. member has said that we should never have embarked upon aiding the Canadian Northern railway at all. The Canadian Northern is an old line and was begun before the Grand Trunk Pacific was ever thought off. Its chances of paying are infinitely better. It is a well placed road both in the West, and in a good many parts of the East. And it must be remembered that in building this road, we are building for the future, and it was thought that Canada could support at least two transeontinentals. I believe it can. I believe that two transeontinentals can be made to pay and pay well, whether operated by private companies or as Government enterprises under a commission. Por my own part, I want to say that it is war time, and the amount of money required to take possession of all the railways of Canada, or even of the railways leaving out the Canadian Pacific, is so great that we cannot afford to undertake it, and that is my only reason, speaking as a business man, for not advocating the immediate nationalization of all the railways of Canada. I may be wrong, but I venture the opinion, as a business man, that with proper management, and with a thoroughly well trained commission of railway men-not politicians, not statesmen even, but railway men of a practical order, such as we have in Canada -the operation of these roads will be successful. In my judgment, if a board was got together, of five or seven of the best railway men in Canada, as a commission and all the roads of Canada were placed at their disposal, they could make a financial and a business success of that great enterprise, I may be wrong but that is my sizing up of the situation. Knowing the possibilities of traffic in Canada I say that I believe that that can be done, and the Drayton-Acworth report practically recommends that that be done. I can hardly do better
than read that part of their report dealing with how these railways should be operated:
Our formal recommendations are:-	*
1.	That a Board of Trustees be constituted by Act of Parliament and incorporated as "The Dominion Railway Company."
2.	That the ownership of the Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk, and Grand Trunk Pacific railways be vested in this Company.
I presume they mean the Transcontinental, as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific.
3.	That the Government assume responsibility to the Company for the interest on the existing securities of these undertakings.
4.	That the Intercolonial (including the Prince Edward Island) and National Transcontinental railways be also handed over by the Government to the Company.
5.	That the whole of these railways, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Intercolonial, and the National Transcontinental, be operated by the Company as one united system.
I must say that that recommendation appeals to me as sound common sense. I do not know these gentlemen personally, but after looking over their report, and having seen the basis upon which they make up all their figures, I believe that that finding is the solution of the railway question facing the Dominion at the present time. As far as I am concerned, just as soon as the war is over, I would be prepared to back up this, or any other, government which is prepared to take hold of this railway situation, face it as it is and make a success of it as a great national enterprise. I may be over optimistic, but I believfe we have as good railway men in Canada as there are anywhere in the world, and nobody need tell me that we cannot get five or seven directors or trustees, whatever they may be called, who can operate the railways of Canada and make them a paying enterprise. My only reason for not advocating the immediate carrying out of these recommendations is that the war is on us, and the question is too large. I was favourable last year to the action taken by the Government in taking over the Canadian Northern. I am still of the same opinion, arid it is my judgment that even if some blunders have been 'made in it, and though some of the money probably has been unwisely expended, we have in the Canadian Northern an asset worth all it is going to' cost the people of Canada, whether we have to pay this supposed ten millions of dollars or not. I do not want to shirk any part of my responsibility in advocating that the $10,000,000 should be, paid if the Commission of Arbitration find that it should be paid. I do not believe in confiscating property, even

though you have technically the right to do so, if there is really an equity in it, and the- Arbitration Commission is sitting for the purpose of deciding whether or not there is any equity in that $60,000,000 of stock, with the understanding that it shall not cost us more than $10,000,000. Is it not best to be generous and fair? I do not know who will get this money, I have no more knowledge than any mem/ber sitting in this House as to whom that $10,000,000 will be paid if awarded, and I do not believe all of it will be awarded. But I do not think we are justified in stating that that stock is not worth a dollar, when the question of its value is being investigated in the courts by some of the best brains in Canada.
We ought to possess our souls in patience, realizing that they will make a just finding and that we shall not have to pay any more for it than the equity in it is worth. I believe that had the Canadian Pacific been given the opportunity of getting the road for $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 and assuming all its liabilities, they would not have taken twenty-four hours to decide that they would accept it. Gentlemen in this House wanted to see the road go under the hammer, to see it knocked down to the highest bidder. They knew that the Canadian Pacific was. the only bidder, and that the Canadian Pacific would not have hesitated a moment to take the road. Had we permitted anything like that to happen, we could not have looked the people of western Canada in the face. We have spent a thousand millions in giving the West railway competition, and it is suggested that now, at the final stage, for the sake of $10,000,000 or $20,000,000, we should let this road merge with the other great railway corporations and destroy competition and all possibility of competition in that country for the next twenty-five or fifty years. In my judgment, the Transcontinental will not be run as a paying enterprise within the life of any hon. gentleman in this House. I do not believe it is possible. More than a thousand miles built in the wilderness, without the slightest traffic- without any passenger traffic at all to speak of along the whole of that route; a bridge at Quebec which cost $27,000,000; a railway which, according to the statement of the Prime Minister this afternoon, cost $90,000 per mile without interest or $110,000 per mile with interest, more than double the cost per mile of the Canadian Northern railway and almost double the cost per mile of the Canadian Pacific [DOT] railway.
[Mr. Cockshutt.l
We have every opportunity, I believe, of making the Canadian Northern a paying enterprise. I congratulate the Government on the splendid stand they have taken in this matter. I was elected as a kind of independent, so to speak, and I have criticised the Government; but when they do a good thing I want to give them credit for it. I stand by them to-night in the bargain that they have made with the Canadian Northern railway. They are facing this question like men. The position that the Prime Minister took in this House to-day and the statement that he made with regard to the Canadian Northern railway -has put him up one hundred per cent in my estimation of him as a business man. I never thought that he was a very good business man, but the way he has tackled the railway question and the manner in which he has placed it before the House and the country gives us reassurance. At last the railway question is to be grappled with. We are to have a policy that we need not be ashamed of, the final financial results of which will be satisfactory not only to be members of the House" but to all the people of Canada.
At this late hour of the night-

In other words the bopk value of the railroad was increased almost three-quarters of a million dollars because the company had to sell its debentures at less than par and by an improper system of bookkeeping that amount was charged up to capital account.
As I have said, the problem we have to face is-where are we going and why are we going in that direction? Surely the experience of the last ten years has taught us that private ownership and the exploitation of the credit of the country has led to one of the most unfortunate railroad muddles the world has ever had to solve, and it comes on Canada at a particularly unfortunate time. We are not saying to the promoters of the railroad: We want to take away your property. We are not confiscating the property at all, but time and again they have represented to this Government and to the country at large that, if we made them an alleged sufficient grant or guarantee or a new loan, they would be able to meet their obligations, and Canada would no longer be called upon to supply further aid. There is not one of us who does not know how repeatedly we have been disappointed. I sat in this House in 1911, 1912, 1913 and 1914, and each year there was a fresh claim and an equally emphatic protest that, if Parliament yielded to the exploiters or promoters, if the hon. members like that term better, it would be the last time they would ask for money, and the undertaking would be carried to a successful conclusion. In 1914, my spirit rebelled, and I laid down what I thought was a sound principle of public guidance, namely, that if the people of Canada had'to pay for a railroad, then the people of Canada were entitled to own it. In 1914, I was opposed to giving further aid, and the reason of my entering into this discussion to-night is because the hon. member for Springfield was rather severe on some of us for voting last year for the arbitration in reference to $60,000,000 worth of Canadian Northern stock. In 1914, I was opposed to Canada going into partnership with Mackenzie and Mann interests in the ownership - and management of the Canadian Northern, and I felt that we were going into partnership in 1914 when we took $40,000,000 worth of theiT stock and left $60,000,000 of the stock to the promoters or to the Mackenzie and Mann interests, because my reading of history has told me this-and if the gentle-

men present in this House care to read history-they will realize this-that when any kind of financial difficulty arises in regard to a large national undertaking, the private persons responsible for that undertaking always assert that Canada has a partnership in the undertaking, and that there is a national obligation to protect the credit of those who venture their capital in a speculative undertaking. For that reason I was opposed in 1914 to the partnership, but at that time public ownership was not as popular as it is to-day, and there was not as much cheering in the House of Commons when those of us who were in favour of t public ownership and public operation of the road advocated those principles as now greets those who rise to speak on the subject. Parliament, however, decided that the partnership was to be, and the arrangement was that $45,000,000 of the Canadian Northern bonds were to be guaranteed, for which Canada was to receive $40,000,000 oi the stock, the balance of $60,000,000 remaining with the owners. The probabilities are that if the war had not broken out, the cash on hand in the Canadian Northern treasuries at that time and the guarantee of the $45,000,000 of bonds would have permitted the Canadian Northern railway to work its way to a successful conclusion. Parliament laid down the principle that Canada was prepared to go into the partnership. Some of us voted against it, but then it seemed to me unfair in 1917 that those who had lent money on the stock of the company and those who had made advances on the bonds of the company should have their securities ruined because a war had unexpectedly broken out, and it was impossible for those behind the undertaking to realize what in ordinary times they would have been able to realize from their debentures and to proceed with the work as they would ordinarily have been able to proceed with it. If the Canadian Pacific were willing to say to the Canadian Northern, as I understand they were: " We are prepared to give something substantial for your stock if you are prepared to hand it over to us," and if the Parliament of Canada was not prepared to give the privilege of selling, it would have been confiscation of the rankest and most indefensible kind for Canada to say to the Canadian Northern people: You cannot sell to the Canadian Pacific, and as we are in a position to refuse you the right of selling, and are also in a position to take your property, we are going to ' take it for nothing, although another company is prepared to

give you a substantial price for it. That would be a confiscation and doing a grave injustice and practising a national irregularity in reference to those who, in good faith, had made advances on the stock and other securities of the Canadian Northern. For that reason I feel the vote I gave in 1917 was justifiable; but even if it were not justifiable, upon that ground, I was quite willing to pay a substantial sum to remove from the lobbies of this Parliament men who,exercise a pernicious influence, and to begin what I thought was the nationalization of the railways of Canada, because I cannot as a Canadian .see-and I have faith in this country and am proud of Canadian ability, character and energy-why we cannot develop in. this country just as capable, honest and energetic men as other countries can develop, and if all the rest of the world, with the exception of the United States and Great Britain, can successfully carry on commission operated railways, 1 am utterly at a loss to see why railways cannot be similarly operated in Canada. In speaking of that matter to-night, the hou. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) reflected sbmewh.at on the Australian railway system. He drew the attention of the House, as an evidence of the mismanagement of that system, to the fact that Australia had different gauges of railways, and he, therefore, from that seemed to argue that the Australian system was a failure.
When the railroads first began in Canada and different charters were granted to different'companies, many of them started out on the same principle :as actuated Australia. They started out with a different gauge of railway, each thinking that in that way it would retain freight originating on its own lines and prevent its transference to another line. Experience very quickly taught us that in a country as widespread as Canada it was absolutely necessary that for facility of transportation the gauges should be standardized and various methods were adopted to bring about that result. Without presenting the matter detail by detail the final result was this: We agreed on a standard gauge of 4 feet 81 inches or 4 feet 81 inches as the proper gauge, and to-day that is practically the gauge adopted throughout Canada. I understand that exactly the same thing is taking place in Australia that took place in Canada. The railways were originally constructed by different states with different gauges but now that they are under the Commonwealth 130J
I was told by a gentleman from Australia whom I had the pleasure of meeting two years ago that they realized that to work out their system they must standardize their gauge and they are doing exactly what Canada did. In the doing of it, of course, there is inconvenience, hut from what I learned from this gentleman with whom I spoke, they are making a success of their roads even under the disadvantages under which they are working at the present time, and they are satisfied that when the work is completed they will work with greater economy and with greater advantage to the Commonwealth at large.
I therefore come to this: we have to face the situation of doing either one of two things. We have got to meet the annual deficits the railroads in Canada are going to have for many years and leave them in the hands of promoters, or we have to take over the roads and run them ourselves. I say that in 1917 we laid down the principle that all Canadian Northern stock was to be acquired by the Canadian people. Having acquired that stock, practically speaking, the people of Canada will own the Canadian Northern. We already own the National Transcontinental, the Prince Edward Island railway, and the Intercolonial railway. The Canadian Northern has a magnificent network of lines in the western provinces, though weak in the eastern part of Canada, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, where the Grand Trunk is strong. Many Canadian Northern lines parallel Grand Trunk lines. I am using " Grand Trunk " in the generic term including various departments of that railway. If we can co-ordinate these roads it is going to cheapen operation by reducing overhead and maintenance charges. Now why not do it? I quite admit that if the situation was this, that the Grand Trunk were able to carry out their undertaking it would be considered confiscation and a breach of the national obligation to interfere arbitrarily with them, but that is not the position in Canada to-day. Canada is not saying to the Grand Trunk Eailway, "We are going to have your road and are not going to pay you for it." But the Grand Trunk management are saying to Canada, "We cannot carry the obligations we undertook by solemn contract. You have taken the National Transcontinental from us and we say we are relieved of all obligation for its operation. We appreciate the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific is on our hack and we cannot get rid of it. We appreciate the fact that if you insist that we carry out our obligations under the contract of 1903 there

is (bound to 'be an insolvency." You ask me on what I base that statement. I base it on the evidence given by Mr. Chamberlin, set out in the appendix to the Drayton-AowoTth report, where in his examination- and the risk a man always runs when he puts himself on oath is that people will believe him even if it turns out to his disadvantage afterwards to be believed-Mr. Chamberlin said, and surely if we in the Parliament of Canada take Mr. Chamberlin as meaning what he said, he should not complain and say we are doing anything we should not do:
Sir Henry Drayton:	You speak of confiscation, in your letter, Mr. Chamberlin. No person is thinking of confiscating the investment that I know of. if you can afford to carry it, you will be allowed to carry It. That was not really meant, was it? Suppose you are left to yourselves, the thing crashes, no one confiscates it. Isn't that right?
Mr. Chamberlin:	To a certain extent, yes.
Sir Henry Drayton:	To every extent, isn't
it?
Mr. Chamberlin:	To every extent.
There we have Mr. Chamberlin's own evidence that the position, of the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific is this: That if the Government does not come to the aid of the Grand Trunk the whole scheme is going to cOme down in insolvency, not only the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the old Grand Trunk itself. The, reason I allude to this particular point is this: I read an extract cabled a few days ago from one of the English papers to the effect that at the annual meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders bitter denouncement had been made of the Canadian Government in that the shareholders had been led to believe that the Canadian people were confiscating the Grand Trunk railway, whereas if the facts had been fairly and squarely put before them, they would have known the Canadian people were not confiscating the Grand Trunk, but that the Grand Trunk Railway Company had admitted to the Government and the people of Canada that they were not able to carry out their obligation, and that there was bound 'to be an insolvency if Canada did not go to the rescue. Canada has a right to be put in a proper light before the investers of the Old World, and I sincerely hope that some echo of what is being said here to-night will be heard across the water. The position the Grand Trunk find themselves in to-day is not the fault of the Canadian people, but the fault of the promoters and exploiters of the national credit. The reason I say that is this. They began in 1903 the movement for the establishment

and development of the National Transcontinental railway. The Government of Canada, headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, did not go to the Grand Trunk Railway, but Mr. Hays came to Sir Wilfrid Laurier with a proposition. He suggested that the Grand Trunk railway in the eastern part of Canada wanted a western connection,. I am ready to admit that the original proposition took the road only as far as North Bay, and that in Parliament it was extended from North Bay down as far as Quebec, and subsequently the Grand Trunk were compelled to accept an extension of the line from Quebec to Moncton. But the Grand Trunk were not compelled to accept it in the sense that they had to enter into an obligation they did not approve of. They could have said, "If the Parliament and 'Government desire us to go so far we will throw up the whole thing," But they did nothing of the sort. They had the choice of doing one of two things, abandoning the enterprise or carrying it out as Parliament desired. The Grand Trunk accepted the terms of the Parliament of Canada and as Mr. Chamberlin said in his evidence-I shall not give his exact words because it is getting late-the contract was utterly impossible for the company to carry out to a successful fruition, the Grand Trunk eould not carry out the scheme, Mr. Chamberlin did not wish to reflect on those who had gone before hut he was uhable to see how Mr. Hays had ever entered into the contract believing it would be a success. He said " it was always impossible." I therefore say the people of Canada are not responsible for the difficulty in which the Grand Trunk find themselves to-night. The Grand Trunk itself, by its improper contract, by lack of foresight on the part of its officials and lack of business vision put the Grand Trunk in the position it is in to-day, and as a Canadian subject, and as a taxpayer I object, to the offspring of the Grand Trunk Railway Company being put in a basket and left on my doorstep, and the railway ringing the bell and saying: "Take charge of the basket and assume the responsibility." I have every desire to protect the credit of Canada, and I say that the Prime Minister if he carries on negotiations this summer with the Grand Trunk shareholders should make it perfectly clear to them and to the people of England that the obligation of the Canadian people was discharged to the last dollar, that Canada did more than she promised to do, that we agreed to guarantee a certain number of bonds and we did it,

that we agreed to build a road and we did it and more.
One hon. gentleman has said that the people of Canada were primarily re-spopsi-ble for whatever sums were spent on building the National Transcontinental. I dissent from that view. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, all of whose stock is owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, had by their agreement with the Government the right to have their engineers superintend the construction of the Transcontinental, and if for political or other reasons their engineers and directors or their management were supine, it is hot the fault of Canada if the road cost more than it should, and the blame should not be laid at the door of Canada.
I want to direct the attention of the House to another point. Somebody has stated that the Government was to blame because Canada gave aid to the Canadian Northern railway after the arrangement had been made with the Grand Trunk for the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Government was not a partner in the undertaking as the Grand Trunk directors assert. The Government agreed that the people of Canada would do a certain thing in assisting this undertaking. The Government have done everything they promised to do and the Government of Canada are, and have always been, a Governement and not a partner. If the Grand Trunk management were not astute enough to protect themselves against the competition of another national transcontinental railway I do not think that they can lay it to the Government and the people that there has been any lack of faith or any bad faith, in the fact that aid was granted to another railway. I am not defending the giving of aid to the Canadian Northern subsequent to the inauguration of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific project. I think it was a mistaken policy. It would have been infinitely wiser if the Grand Trunk had purchased the Canadian Northern line. But if the members of this House want some evidence of the money that exploiters and promoters attempt to make out of railway construction let me direct their attention to another portion of the evidence of Mr. Chamberlin. Sir Henry Drayton asked Mr. Chamberlin this question as reported at page 80 of the Drayton-Acworth report:
Sir Henry Drayton: If I am not very much mistaken, negotiations were entered into between your executive and the executive of the
Canadian Northern, looking to the fusion of the systems, so that there would not he this clupU-cation.	.
Mr. Chamberlin: They tried to buy the Manitoba lines, but they could not get together, Mr. Hays told me at one time, and Mr. Wainwright told me also. I asked them why they did not buy out the Canadian Northern, they said they had had meeting after meeting with them, and that the best terms they could get were that they should assume all obligations, all bonds and everything else, and give $2-5,0-00,000 for the common stock for that little bunch of lines up around Winnipeg.
That meant that the Canadian Northern people asked the Grand Trunk to pay them $25,000,000 for the common stock which they held. That will give you some idea of the exploitation that has been attempted in this country. I think it well that the people should realize what private ownership has done in connection with railway promotion. People had hardly come to realize the terrific problem tha-t confronted ue in this country before a private Bill was again introduced into this House in the session of 1915 asking Parliament to grant a charter to another transcontinental railway and it was only because of the
1 a.m. active efforts of those opposed to Canada being loaded up with any further lines that the charter was withdrawn and the promotion stopped. For these reasons I think the time has come for the taking over of those lines. The experience of the world has demonstrated that it is possible to get able, honest men to operate public utilities such as railways. We have demonstrated that in regard- to lighting and power plants and in various other ways. And if these things can be done by other public bodies why cannot the same thing be done in reference to- a railway?
Then, let us regard it from another angle. The main object to be sought is- to procure adequate transportation for the people and commodities of the country. It must be abundantly clear to any person- who has read this report, and who knows anything of the railway situation in Canada-and certainly the , hon. member from East Al-goma (Mr. Nicholson) put a mass of illuminating figures on the record to-night- that the railways have reached the point where they are utterly unable to raise the necessary capital to carry on their undertakings. It is admitted that the Canadian Northern Railway system cannot raise the $100,000,000 that they need in the next five years to bring their road up to the standard necessary in connection with a road seeking to undertake transportation in Canada. Well, there are one or
two points I want to clear up, and as honourable gentlemen have expressed the wish for me to go on, perhaps it is just as well that I should touch on those points.
Now in regard to the Intercolonial, that railway is always held up by opposing Canadians as the outstanding example of a failure of Government ownership. But is that fair? The Intercolonial was a political railroad. It was constructed round by the St. Lawrence so that it would be well removed from the American border. It was a political road and it was a military road. Every car mile that is operated on that road costs more money to run in relation to the earnings got than if it were a direct line. What I mean by that is this:	The railroad is
operated on the arc of a circle, but the freight charge must be in competition with the rate charged on the diameter of the circle. That is, for a very much larger mileage the Intercolonial gets only the smaller freight charged on the straight line, and while I have not the figures before me to-night-not intending to speak on this subject-I was much impressed some years ago by an examination of the figures which showed to me conclusively that the car mile freight on the Intercolonial was smaller by far than that charged on the other railroads. And that simply means this: That every extra mile you operate a railroad	to carry freight	means that
much	extra cost that the railroad
has to pay for operation-wages, coal, upkeep, and everything that is included in the operation of a railroad-and if a railroad is unnecessarily long, and only earning freight proportionate to a shorter railroad, certainly it is never going to be comparatively a success. If in conjunction with that fact you take the fact that the people of the eastern provinces have always regarded the Intercolonial as a quid pro quo for the canals in the central part, of the country, and incidentally used for the transportation of the western commodities to the seaboard, I do not think it is surprising that the railroad has not been a great success. Then, too, being a political railway, political considerations have entered into its operation, with the result that the road has not made money. Therefore, I say it is not an outstanding example of the' failure of public operation, 'but is an example of how a badly situated road cannot be a profitable work, and must of necessity be a financial failure, when burdened further as I have explained.
I agree with what the hon. member for East Algoma said, that if after these railroads are taken over-I am talking of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk system-you are going to operate them successfully, you have got to co-ordinate them, you have got to remove all unnecessary overhead charges, you have got to get rid of parallel lines, and you have got to insist that between the Canadian Pacific and these co-ordinated Government lines there shall be co-operation and control of rates through the railway commission. I do not believe the time is ripe for the taking over of the Canadian Pacific Railway system: If I understand the position of the Canadian Pacific railway, they would have a right, if the Parliament of Canada insisted there should be nationalization, that the assets of the Canadian Pacific Railway system be taken over at their value, and men who are in a position to speak-I do not profess to speak of my own knowledge-tell me that if the assets of the Canadian Pacific were taken over at reconstruction value Canada would have to practically pay $800,000,000 for the undertaking, and it would nece3>-sitate an increase in freight rates of twenty to thirty per cent probably on the rates now charged. It would be impossible for Canada to do anything of that sort.
The -Canadian Pacific railway is financially strong, and it is well run, and, as I said in the beginning of my remarks, the object of Canada at this critical time must be the protection of her credit, while securing adequate transportation facilities, and if in competition with Government-owned roads and publicly-managed roads- the Canadian Pacific railway is in a sufficiently strong position to stand the competition and to operate the road as a financial success, then why should Canada load herself up at a critical time like this with $800,000,000 which she can avoid? It seems to me it would be an unwise thing to do, and unwise for another reason: If the Canadian Pacific were taken over by the Government of Canada it would remove that tremendous asset as a borrowing security when fresh capital is going to be required for the development of this country. The Canadian Pacific railway to-day has a great place in the financial markets of the world, her credit is on the soundest basis. But if the road were taken over by the Government of Canada it would not add

one dollar to the credit power of the Canadian people as a people, but would remove that credit power from one of the. greatest combinations thait the world has ever known, as well as scattering abroad the capital represented by the stock and securities. For these reasons I think it would be unwise at the present time to take over the Canadian Pacific railway. Let us take no more steps at the present than we, must take, but let us take such steps as are nationally necessary to secure for the Canadian people the properties that they are going to be called upon to carry in any event. Let us take such steps as will lessen the cost of transportation, that will cut out unnecessary duplication, and that will co-ordinate under one system m Canada these two roads that are at present a financial failure. Let us try to see to it that some scheme of operation is developed by which political interference will be avoided, that the maximum efficiency will 'be secured, and that we at length will take one great forward step in solving the problem that has been forced upon us, not by the choice of the Canadian people, but perhaps through the lack of vision of her statesmen and Parliamentarians. Let us take this step now in the interest of the national life of Canada, but let us make clear to the world that while we are taking this step we are not confiscating the property of other people, but that wre are dealing fairly with them, that we are relieving them, from obligations they have voluntarily entered into, and that if there is difficulty in the administration of their railroads and undertakings, those difficulties have not been brought about by the niggardliness, not by the parsimony, and not by the necessities of the Canadian people, but by the directors and others responsible for the administration of these great undertakings and from their lack of foresight and appreciation of the conditions that prevail in this country.
I suggest that the committee rise now and that the House adjourn.
